    Reference

    225 Functions

    Each call is the shared name and argument order. C, PHP, Python, and Dart use that same order. Output arguments are buffers you allocate. A status return is JME_OK or JME_ERR . The line under the name says what the call does, when to choose it, and where it sits in a program.

    This box filters the function list. The sidebar search looks through the whole page and highlights each match.

    Function group

    Angles and Formatting

    Use these after you already have a number. They wrap, compare, or print an angle, a clock time, or a duration. They do not compute a planet.

    jme_centiseconds_to_lonlat_string

    What it does Formats a signed centisecond angle as a degree-style longitude or latitude string.

    When to use it Use this to print a geographic or ecliptic angle you stored in centiseconds.

    Where it fits Display only.

    Call jme_centiseconds_to_lonlat_string(cs, buffer)
    Arguments
    • cs Angle or time in centiseconds. A full circle or a day of time is 1,296,000 centiseconds.
    • buffer Caller-owned character buffer. The call writes the text here.
    Result

    Returns the text. When you pass buffer, the text is written there and the return points at that buffer.

    jme_decimal_hour

    What it does Turns hours, minutes, and seconds into a decimal hour.

    When to use it Use this before jme_julian_day, which takes one hour number.

    Where it fits Clock entry.

    Call jme_decimal_hour(hour, minute, second)
    Arguments
    • hour Whole hours.
    • minute Whole minutes.
    • second Seconds, including a fraction.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_centiseconds_difference

    What it does Returns the separation of two centisecond angles.

    When to use it Use this to test whether two longitudes stored in centiseconds have met.

    Where it fits Angle storage. The signed form keeps the direction.

    Call jme_centiseconds_difference(p1, p2)
    Arguments
    • p1 First angle in centiseconds.
    • p2 Second angle in centiseconds.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_centiseconds_difference_signed

    What it does Returns the signed separation of two centisecond angles.

    When to use it Use this when the direction around the circle matters.

    Where it fits The unsigned pair is jme_centiseconds_difference.

    Call jme_centiseconds_difference_signed(p1, p2)
    Arguments
    • p1 First angle in centiseconds.
    • p2 Second angle in centiseconds.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_centiseconds_normalize

    What it does Wraps a centisecond angle onto one full circle.

    When to use it Use this before you store or compare an angle that may have wound past a full turn.

    Where it fits Any centisecond longitude.

    Call jme_centiseconds_normalize(p)
    Arguments
    • p Angle in centiseconds to wrap onto one full circle.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_centiseconds_round_second

    What it does Rounds a centisecond angle to the nearest whole second.

    When to use it Use this only for display rounding. Do not feed it back into a calculation you want at full precision.

    Where it fits A printed degree-minute-second field.

    Call jme_centiseconds_round_second(x)
    Arguments
    • x Centiseconds to round to the nearest whole second.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_jd_difference_seconds

    What it does Returns the signed number of seconds from one Julian date to another.

    When to use it Use this to measure a duration between two instants you already hold as Julian dates.

    Where it fits jd_end minus jd_start, in seconds.

    Call jme_jd_difference_seconds(jd_end, jd_start)
    Arguments
    • jd_end End Julian date.
    • jd_start Julian date to search from. The matching time scale is the one in the function name.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    Function group

    Configuration and Utilities

    Call these at setup, or when you need an orbital element set. They change or read a library setting that later calculations inherit.

    jme_close

    What it does Releases resources the library is holding, including an open kernel.

    When to use it Call it when the process is finished with ephemeris calls.

    Where it fits Shutdown. Later calls need a new setup.

    Call jme_close()
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_get_orbital_elements

    What it does Writes the orbital elements of a body at Terrestrial Time.

    When to use it Use this when you need the element set itself, not a longitude.

    Where it fits An orbit panel. flags follow the calculation flags.

    Call jme_get_orbital_elements(jd_et, body, flags, elem, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_et Terrestrial Time (TT) as a Julian date.
    • body Body id such as JME_BODY_SUN. The body constants list every id.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • elem Caller-owned array of orbital elements.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_set_astro_models

    What it does Sets engine and model tokens for later calculations.

    When to use it Call it at startup to choose JPL, Moshier, VSOP plus ELP, or AUTO, and to name precession or nutation models.

    Where it fits Before jme_calc. The checked form rejects an unknown token and leaves the old setting in place.

    Call jme_set_astro_models(models, flags)
    Arguments
    • models Text tokens such as ENGINE=JPL or ENGINE=MOSHIER. The engine section lists the tokens.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_get_astro_models

    What it does Writes the current model tokens into models.

    When to use it Call it to show or save the active engine and model choices.

    Where it fits After jme_set_astro_models.

    Call jme_get_astro_models(models, flags)
    Arguments
    • models Text tokens such as ENGINE=JPL or ENGINE=MOSHIER. The engine section lists the tokens.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_set_lapse_rate

    What it does Sets the temperature lapse rate used by extended refraction.

    When to use it Call it when the observer is high enough that sea-level weather is the wrong profile.

    Where it fits Before jme_refract_extended, if you do not pass the lapse on that call.

    Call jme_set_lapse_rate(lapse_rate)
    Arguments
    • lapse_rate Temperature lapse rate. jme_refract_extended uses it when the observer is not at sea level.
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_set_interpolate_nut

    What it does Turns nutation interpolation on or off for later orientation calls.

    When to use it Use this only when you deliberately want the interpolated nutation series.

    Where it fits A setup call. Leave it off unless you know you want that interpolation.

    Call jme_set_interpolate_nut(on)
    Arguments
    • on Non-zero turns the option on. Zero turns it off.
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_get_tid_acc

    What it does Returns the tidal acceleration currently applied to historical Delta-T.

    When to use it Call it to record which JME_TIME_TIDAL_* choice is active.

    Where it fits After jme_set_tid_acc.

    Call jme_get_tid_acc()
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_set_tid_acc

    What it does Selects the tidal acceleration used with historical Delta-T.

    When to use it Call it when a JPL ephemeris requires its matching tidal value. JME_TIME_TIDAL_DE441 has no published historical acceleration, so pre-1955 Delta-T then returns a non-finite value and an error.

    Where it fits Setup, before long-range Delta-T. JME_TIME_TIDAL_AUTOMATIC applies no extra correction.

    Call jme_set_tid_acc(t_acc)
    Arguments
    • t_acc Tidal acceleration selector, usually a JME_TIME_TIDAL_* constant, or a numeric acceleration when you set one directly.
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_days_in_month

    What it does Returns how many days the month has in that year and calendar.

    When to use it Use this to build a month grid or to cap a day field.

    Where it fits Date entry.

    Call jme_days_in_month(year, month, calendar)
    Arguments
    • year Calendar year. Astronomical year numbering, so 1 BCE is year 0.
    • month Month number from 1 to 12.
    • calendar JME_CALENDAR_GREGORIAN or JME_CALENDAR_JULIAN.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_refract

    What it does Applies atmospheric refraction to an altitude angle.

    When to use it Use this to turn a true altitude into an apparent one, or the reverse, at the observer's pressure and temperature.

    Where it fits calc_flag JME_COORD_APPARENT_TO_TRUE subtracts refraction. JME_COORD_TRUE_TO_APPARENT adds it. Below about -1 degree, or with no pressure, the altitude is returned unchanged.

    Call jme_refract(altitude, pressure, temperature, calc_flag)
    Arguments
    • altitude Altitude angle in degrees.
    • pressure Air pressure in millibars. The sea-level default used by the refraction formula is 1010.
    • temperature Air temperature in degrees Celsius.
    • calc_flag JME_COORD_APPARENT_TO_TRUE removes refraction. JME_COORD_TRUE_TO_APPARENT adds it.
    Result

    Returns the corrected altitude in degrees. Extended refraction also fills out when you pass it.

    jme_refract_extended

    What it does Applies refraction with observer height and a lapse rate, and can return the intermediate weather.

    When to use it Use this when the observer is not at the pressure you measured at sea level.

    Where it fits out, when present, receives corrected altitude, refraction, local pressure, and local temperature.

    Call jme_refract_extended(altitude, geoalt, pressure, temperature, lapse_rate, calc_flag, out)
    Arguments
    • altitude Altitude angle in degrees.
    • geoalt Observer height in metres, used to adjust pressure and temperature.
    • pressure Air pressure in millibars. The sea-level default used by the refraction formula is 1010.
    • temperature Air temperature in degrees Celsius.
    • lapse_rate Temperature lapse rate. jme_refract_extended uses it when the observer is not at sea level.
    • calc_flag JME_COORD_APPARENT_TO_TRUE removes refraction. JME_COORD_TRUE_TO_APPARENT adds it.
    • out Optional extra outputs. For extended refraction this is four numbers: corrected altitude, refraction, local pressure, local temperature.
    Result

    Returns the corrected altitude in degrees. Extended refraction also fills out when you pass it.

    Function group

    Coordinates and Vectors

    Use these when you already have a place or a Cartesian state and you need another frame: ecliptic, equator, horizon, or a rotation matrix.

    jme_centiseconds_to_degree_string

    What it does Formats a centisecond angle as a degree string.

    When to use it Use this for the same stored angle when you want degrees rather than a coordinate sign convention.

    Where it fits Display only.

    Call jme_centiseconds_to_degree_string(cs, buffer)
    Arguments
    • cs Angle or time in centiseconds. A full circle or a day of time is 1,296,000 centiseconds.
    • buffer Caller-owned character buffer. The call writes the text here.
    Result

    Returns the text. When you pass buffer, the text is written there and the return points at that buffer.

    jme_get_obliquity

    What it does Returns the obliquity of the ecliptic at Terrestrial Time for a chosen model.

    When to use it Use this when a house or coordinate call asks you to supply eps, or when you want to display it.

    Where it fits Pass the result into the RAMC house calls.

    Call jme_get_obliquity(jd_et, model, eps, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_et Terrestrial Time (TT) as a Julian date.
    • model Model id from the JME_MODEL_* or JME_SIDEREAL_* constants, depending on the call.
    • eps Obliquity of the ecliptic, in degrees, at the date you are using.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_get_frame_bias_matrix

    What it does Writes the frame-bias rotation for a bias model.

    When to use it Use this when you rotate vectors between the catalogue frame and the equinox yourself.

    Where it fits Before your own matrix multiply. m is nine numbers.

    Call jme_get_frame_bias_matrix(model, m)
    Arguments
    • model Model id from the JME_MODEL_* or JME_SIDEREAL_* constants, depending on the call.
    • m Caller-owned rotation matrix, nine numbers, row by row.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_get_nutation

    What it does Returns nutation in longitude and obliquity at Terrestrial Time.

    When to use it Use this when you apply nutation yourself, or when you need those angles for apparent sidereal time.

    Where it fits dpsi and deps receive the two angles.

    Call jme_get_nutation(jd_et, model, dpsi, deps, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_et Terrestrial Time (TT) as a Julian date.
    • model Model id from the JME_MODEL_* or JME_SIDEREAL_* constants, depending on the call.
    • dpsi Receives nutation in longitude.
    • deps Receives nutation in obliquity.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_get_precession_matrix

    What it does Writes the precession rotation from one TT date to another.

    When to use it Use this to move a vector between two epochs.

    Where it fits m is nine numbers. The model selects the precession series.

    Call jme_get_precession_matrix(jd_start, jd_end, model, m)
    Arguments
    • jd_start TT Julian date at the start of the precession interval.
    • jd_end TT Julian date at the end of the precession interval.
    • model Model id from the JME_MODEL_* or JME_SIDEREAL_* constants, depending on the call.
    • m Caller-owned rotation matrix, nine numbers, row by row.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_get_nutation_matrix

    What it does Builds the nutation matrix from nutation angles and obliquity, in radians.

    When to use it Use this after jme_get_nutation when you need the matrix rather than the two angles.

    Where it fits A coordinate pipeline you are writing yourself.

    Call jme_get_nutation_matrix(dpsi_rad, deps_rad, eps_rad, m)
    Arguments
    • dpsi_rad Nutation in longitude, in radians.
    • deps_rad Nutation in obliquity, in radians.
    • eps_rad Obliquity, in radians.
    • m Caller-owned rotation matrix, nine numbers, row by row.
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_matrix_identity

    What it does Writes a 3 by 3 identity matrix.

    When to use it Use this as the starting matrix before you multiply in precession or nutation.

    Where it fits m is nine numbers.

    Call jme_matrix_identity(m)
    Arguments
    • m Caller-owned rotation matrix, nine numbers, row by row.
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_matrix_multiply

    What it does Multiplies two 3 by 3 matrices into out.

    When to use it Use this to combine frame rotations.

    Where it fits A coordinate pipeline. out must not be assumed to alias a or b unless you have checked that.

    Call jme_matrix_multiply(a, b, out)
    Arguments
    • a First rotation matrix, nine numbers.
    • b Second rotation matrix, nine numbers.
    • out Optional extra outputs. For extended refraction this is four numbers: corrected altitude, refraction, local pressure, local temperature.
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_matrix_rotate_x

    What it does Writes the rotation matrix about the x axis.

    When to use it Use this when you build a rotation the library does not already provide.

    Where it fits angle_rad is radians. m receives nine numbers.

    Call jme_matrix_rotate_x(angle_rad, m)
    Arguments
    • angle_rad Rotation angle in radians.
    • m Caller-owned rotation matrix, nine numbers, row by row.
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_matrix_rotate_y

    What it does Writes the rotation matrix about the y axis.

    When to use it Use this for the y component of a rotation you are composing.

    Where it fits Same layout as jme_matrix_rotate_x.

    Call jme_matrix_rotate_y(angle_rad, m)
    Arguments
    • angle_rad Rotation angle in radians.
    • m Caller-owned rotation matrix, nine numbers, row by row.
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_matrix_rotate_z

    What it does Writes the rotation matrix about the z axis.

    When to use it Use this for a rotation in the reference plane, such as a longitude shift you apply yourself.

    Where it fits Same layout as jme_matrix_rotate_x.

    Call jme_matrix_rotate_z(angle_rad, m)
    Arguments
    • angle_rad Rotation angle in radians.
    • m Caller-owned rotation matrix, nine numbers, row by row.
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_degree_midpoint

    What it does Returns the midpoint of two angles in degrees, on the short arc.

    When to use it Use this for the middle of a nakshatra, a house, or an arc.

    Where it fits Both inputs are degrees.

    Call jme_degree_midpoint(x1, x0)
    Arguments
    • x1 First angle in degrees.
    • x0 Second angle in degrees.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_degree_normalize

    What it does Wraps a degree angle onto one full circle.

    When to use it Use this before you compare a longitude with a boundary.

    Where it fits Any ecliptic or equatorial degree measure.

    Call jme_degree_normalize(x)
    Arguments
    • x Angle in degrees to wrap onto one full circle.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_degrees_to_hours

    What it does Converts degrees of angle to hours of right ascension or time.

    When to use it Use this when a sidereal-time or right-ascension field must be shown in hours.

    Where it fits 15 degrees become 1 hour.

    Call jme_degrees_to_hours(degrees)
    Arguments
    • degrees Angle in degrees.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_degrees_to_radians

    What it does Converts degrees to radians.

    When to use it Use this at the boundary of a routine that wants radians, such as the nutation matrix.

    Where it fits The reverse is jme_radians_to_degrees.

    Call jme_degrees_to_radians(degrees)
    Arguments
    • degrees Angle in degrees.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_degrees_difference

    What it does Returns the separation of two degree angles.

    When to use it Use this to measure a house width or a distance along the ecliptic without the sign.

    Where it fits The signed form keeps the direction.

    Call jme_degrees_difference(p1, p2)
    Arguments
    • p1 First angle in degrees.
    • p2 Second angle in degrees.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_degrees_difference_signed

    What it does Returns the signed separation of two degree angles.

    When to use it Use this when you need to know which way the motion goes.

    Where it fits The unsigned pair is jme_degrees_difference.

    Call jme_degrees_difference_signed(p1, p2)
    Arguments
    • p1 First angle in degrees.
    • p2 Second angle in degrees.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_ecliptic_to_equatorial

    What it does Converts ecliptic longitude and latitude to right ascension and declination.

    When to use it Use this when you have an ecliptic place and you need the equator of date.

    Where it fits You supply the obliquity eps. The reverse is jme_equatorial_to_ecliptic.

    Call jme_ecliptic_to_equatorial(lon, lat, eps, ra, dec)
    Arguments
    • lon Longitude in degrees. East is positive when this is a place. For an angle helper it is the ecliptic or equatorial longitude the call names.
    • lat Latitude in degrees. North is positive when this is a place.
    • eps Obliquity of the ecliptic, in degrees, at the date you are using.
    • ra Receives right ascension.
    • dec Declination in degrees, or the variable that receives it.
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_equatorial_to_ecliptic

    What it does Converts right ascension and declination to ecliptic longitude and latitude.

    When to use it Use this when a star or a vector is equatorial and the chart is ecliptic.

    Where it fits You supply eps.

    Call jme_equatorial_to_ecliptic(ra, dec, eps, lon, lat)
    Arguments
    • ra Receives right ascension.
    • dec Declination in degrees, or the variable that receives it.
    • eps Obliquity of the ecliptic, in degrees, at the date you are using.
    • lon Longitude in degrees. East is positive when this is a place. For an angle helper it is the ecliptic or equatorial longitude the call names.
    • lat Latitude in degrees. North is positive when this is a place.
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_spherical_angular_separation

    What it does Returns the great-circle angle between two spherical positions.

    When to use it Use this for the distance on the sky between two longitudes and latitudes.

    Where it fits Conjunction tests and angular separation. The unit is degrees.

    Call jme_spherical_angular_separation(lon1, lat1, lon2, lat2)
    Arguments
    • lon1 Longitude of the first point, in degrees.
    • lat1 Latitude of the first point, in degrees.
    • lon2 Longitude of the second point, in degrees.
    • lat2 Latitude of the second point, in degrees.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_spherical_position_angle

    What it does Returns the position angle of the second point from the first.

    When to use it Use this when you need the direction of one body from another on the sky.

    Where it fits The result is a degree angle.

    Call jme_spherical_position_angle(lon1, lat1, lon2, lat2)
    Arguments
    • lon1 Longitude of the first point, in degrees.
    • lat1 Latitude of the first point, in degrees.
    • lon2 Longitude of the second point, in degrees.
    • lat2 Latitude of the second point, in degrees.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_radian_midpoint

    What it does Returns the midpoint of two radian angles on the short arc.

    When to use it Use this when the surrounding math is already in radians.

    Where it fits The degree form is jme_degree_midpoint.

    Call jme_radian_midpoint(x1, x0)
    Arguments
    • x1 First angle in radians.
    • x0 Second angle in radians.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_radian_normalize

    What it does Wraps a radian angle onto one full turn.

    When to use it Use this before a comparison in radians.

    Where it fits The degree form is jme_degree_normalize.

    Call jme_radian_normalize(x)
    Arguments
    • x Angle in radians to wrap onto one full turn.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_radians_to_degrees

    What it does Converts radians to degrees.

    When to use it Use this to present a radian result in degrees.

    Where it fits The reverse is jme_degrees_to_radians.

    Call jme_radians_to_degrees(radians)
    Arguments
    • radians Angle in radians.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_radians_difference_signed

    What it does Returns the signed separation of two radian angles.

    When to use it Use this when both angles are already in radians and the direction matters.

    Where it fits The degree form is jme_degrees_difference_signed.

    Call jme_radians_difference_signed(p1, p2)
    Arguments
    • p1 First angle in radians.
    • p2 Second angle in radians.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_hours_normalize

    What it does Wraps a time in hours onto one day.

    When to use it Use this after adding hours that may have passed 24.

    Where it fits Sidereal time and decimal hours.

    Call jme_hours_normalize(hours)
    Arguments
    • hours Hours to wrap onto one day.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_hours_to_degrees

    What it does Converts hours of right ascension or time to degrees.

    When to use it Use this when a sidereal time in hours must enter a house call that wants degrees.

    Where it fits 1 hour becomes 15 degrees.

    Call jme_hours_to_degrees(hours)
    Arguments
    • hours Receives sidereal time in hours.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_split_degree

    What it does Splits a decimal degree angle into sign, degrees, minutes, seconds, and the fraction of a second.

    When to use it Use this to print a longitude without building the string yourself.

    Where it fits roundflag ROUND_DEG, ROUND_MIN, or ROUND_SEC chooses the rounding. The other angle-format ids are not applied here.

    Call jme_split_degree(ddeg, roundflag, ideg, imin, isec, dsecfr, isgn)
    Arguments
    • ddeg Angle in decimal degrees to split into sign, degrees, minutes, and seconds.
    • roundflag Rounding choice. JME_ANGLE_FORMAT_ROUND_DEG, ROUND_MIN, or ROUND_SEC. The other format ids are not applied by this call.
    • ideg Receives the degree part.
    • imin Receives the minute part.
    • isec Receives the whole-second part.
    • dsecfr Receives the fraction of the second.
    • isgn Receives the sign: 1 or -1.
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    Function group

    Eclipses and Occultations

    Use these to search for an eclipse or an occultation, or to describe one whose time you already know. A position call will not return contact times.

    jme_sol_eclipse_where

    What it does Finds where on Earth a solar eclipse is central at a Universal Time.

    When to use it Use this when you have a time inside an eclipse and you need the geographic path point.

    Where it fits Global eclipse maps. For the next eclipse, search first with jme_sol_eclipse_when_glob.

    Call jme_sol_eclipse_where(jd_ut, flags, geopos, attr, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • flags Reserved argument; this function currently ignores it. Pass 0.
    • geopos Observer longitude, latitude, and height, in that order, in degrees and metres.
    • attr Caller-owned array that receives the circumstance values for this call.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns a JME_ECLIPSE_SOLAR_* classification on success, or JME_ERR (-1). Test rc < 0 for failure. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_sol_eclipse_how

    What it does Computes how a solar eclipse appears at one place and Universal Time.

    When to use it Use this when the observer is fixed and you want magnitude and the related attributes.

    Where it fits A local eclipse page. geopos is that place.

    Call jme_sol_eclipse_how(jd_ut, flags, geopos, attr, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • flags Reserved argument; this function currently ignores it. Pass 0.
    • geopos Observer longitude, latitude, and height, in that order, in degrees and metres.
    • attr Caller-owned array that receives the circumstance values for this call.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns a JME_ECLIPSE_SOLAR_* classification on success, or JME_ERR (-1). Test rc < 0 for failure. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_sol_eclipse_when_loc

    What it does Searches for the next or previous solar eclipse at one place.

    When to use it Use this when the question is 'when is the eclipse visible here'.

    Where it fits A local calendar. backward searches earlier. tret receives the contact times.

    Call jme_sol_eclipse_when_loc(jd_start, flags, geopos, tret, attr, backward, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_start Julian date to search from. The matching time scale is the one in the function name.
    • flags Reserved argument; this function currently ignores it. Pass 0.
    • geopos Observer longitude, latitude, and height, in that order, in degrees and metres.
    • tret Caller-owned array of Julian dates. The description says which index is which event.
    • attr Caller-owned array that receives the circumstance values for this call.
    • backward Search direction. Non-zero searches before jd_start. Zero searches after it.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns a JME_ECLIPSE_SOLAR_* classification on success, or JME_ERR (-1). Test rc < 0 for failure. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_sol_eclipse_when_glob

    What it does Searches for the next or previous solar eclipse anywhere on Earth.

    When to use it Use this to build a worldwide eclipse list.

    Where it fits Start from jd_start and walk forward, or backward. Then call the where and how functions for a chosen instant.

    Call jme_sol_eclipse_when_glob(jd_start, flags, epheflag, tret, backward, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_start Julian date to search from. The matching time scale is the one in the function name.
    • flags Reserved argument; this function currently ignores it. Pass 0.
    • epheflag Eclipse-type filter: 0 for any, or JME_ECLIPSE_SOLAR_TOTAL, _ANNULAR, _HYBRID, _PARTIAL, _CENTRAL or _NONCENTRAL.
    • tret Caller-owned array of Julian dates. The description says which index is which event.
    • backward Search direction. Non-zero searches before jd_start. Zero searches after it.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns a JME_ECLIPSE_SOLAR_* classification on success, or JME_ERR (-1). Test rc < 0 for failure. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_lun_eclipse_how

    What it does Computes how a lunar eclipse appears at one place and Universal Time.

    When to use it Use this for magnitude and contact data of a lunar eclipse at a known time.

    Where it fits A local lunar-eclipse page.

    Call jme_lun_eclipse_how(jd_ut, flags, geopos, attr, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • flags Reserved argument; this function currently ignores it. Pass 0.
    • geopos Observer longitude, latitude, and height, in that order, in degrees and metres.
    • attr Caller-owned array that receives the circumstance values for this call.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns a JME_ECLIPSE_LUNAR_* classification on success, or JME_ERR (-1). Test rc < 0 for failure. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_lun_eclipse_when_loc

    What it does Searches for the next or previous lunar eclipse at one place.

    When to use it Use this when the observer is fixed.

    Where it fits A local calendar. The global search is jme_lun_eclipse_when.

    Call jme_lun_eclipse_when_loc(jd_start, flags, geopos, tret, attr, backward, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_start Julian date to search from. The matching time scale is the one in the function name.
    • flags Reserved argument; this function currently ignores it. Pass 0.
    • geopos Observer longitude, latitude, and height, in that order, in degrees and metres.
    • tret Caller-owned array of Julian dates. The description says which index is which event.
    • attr Caller-owned array that receives the circumstance values for this call.
    • backward Search direction. Non-zero searches before jd_start. Zero searches after it.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns a JME_ECLIPSE_LUNAR_* classification on success, or JME_ERR (-1). Test rc < 0 for failure. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_lun_eclipse_when

    What it does Searches for the next or previous lunar eclipse worldwide.

    When to use it Use this to list lunar eclipses before you care about one city.

    Where it fits A worldwide eclipse index.

    Call jme_lun_eclipse_when(jd_start, flags, iflag, tret, backward, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_start Julian date to search from. The matching time scale is the one in the function name.
    • flags Reserved argument; this function currently ignores it. Pass 0.
    • iflag Eclipse-type filter: 0 for any, or JME_ECLIPSE_LUNAR_TOTAL, _PARTIAL or _PENUMBRAL.
    • tret Caller-owned array of Julian dates. The description says which index is which event.
    • backward Search direction. Non-zero searches before jd_start. Zero searches after it.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns a JME_ECLIPSE_LUNAR_* classification on success, or JME_ERR (-1). Test rc < 0 for failure. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_lun_occult_where

    What it does Finds where a lunar occultation of a body or star is central at a Universal Time.

    When to use it Use this when the time is known and you need the geographic point.

    Where it fits Occultation maps. starname is empty for a planet.

    Call jme_lun_occult_where(jd_ut, body, starname, flags, geopos, attr, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • body Body id such as JME_BODY_SUN. The body constants list every id.
    • starname Star name. Use an empty string when the call is for a solar-system body.
    • flags Reserved argument; this function currently ignores it. Pass 0.
    • geopos Observer longitude, latitude, and height, in that order, in degrees and metres.
    • attr Caller-owned array that receives the circumstance values for this call.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_lun_occult_when_loc

    What it does Searches for the next or previous occultation by the Moon at one place.

    When to use it Use this for 'when does the Moon cover this body here'.

    Where it fits A local occultation list. Pass the body, or a star name.

    Call jme_lun_occult_when_loc(jd_start, body, starname, flags, geopos, tret, attr, backward, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_start Julian date to search from. The matching time scale is the one in the function name.
    • body Body id such as JME_BODY_SUN. The body constants list every id.
    • starname Star name. Use an empty string when the call is for a solar-system body.
    • flags Reserved argument; this function currently ignores it. Pass 0.
    • geopos Observer longitude, latitude, and height, in that order, in degrees and metres.
    • tret Caller-owned array of Julian dates. The description says which index is which event.
    • attr Caller-owned array that receives the circumstance values for this call.
    • backward Search direction. Non-zero searches before jd_start. Zero searches after it.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_lun_occult_when_glob

    What it does Searches for the next or previous lunar occultation anywhere on Earth.

    When to use it Use this for a worldwide occultation list.

    Where it fits tret[0] is greatest occultation. Indexes 2 and 3 are the outer contacts. Stars are treated as points at infinity.

    Call jme_lun_occult_when_glob(jd_start, body, starname, flags, iflag, tret, backward, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_start Julian date to search from. The matching time scale is the one in the function name.
    • body Body id such as JME_BODY_SUN. The body constants list every id.
    • starname Star name. Use an empty string when the call is for a solar-system body.
    • flags Reserved argument; this function currently ignores it. Pass 0.
    • iflag Reserved search-flag argument; this function currently ignores it.
    • tret Event times. Index 0 is greatest occultation. Indexes 2 and 3 are the first and last contact anywhere on Earth. Indexes 4 and 5 are the total phase when there is one. Indexes 6 and 7 are the central phase when there is one.
    • backward Search direction. Non-zero searches before jd_start. Zero searches after it.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    Function group

    Fixed Stars and Metadata

    Use these for a named star, or for the version and file paths of the library. Star magnitude does not need a date. Star position does.

    jme_version

    What it does Copies the library version string into buffer.

    When to use it Call it once at startup when you need to show or record which JME build is loaded.

    Where it fits Any program, before you trust a result. This release's string is 2.0.0.

    Call jme_version(buffer, buffer_size)
    Arguments
    • buffer Caller-owned character buffer. The call writes the text here.
    • buffer_size Size of buffer, in bytes, including room for the terminating zero.
    Result

    Returns the text. When you pass buffer, the text is written there and the return points at that buffer.

    jme_ephemeris_path

    What it does Returns the directory the library searches for ephemeris files.

    When to use it Call it when you need to show or check the path that was set.

    Where it fits After jme_set_ephemeris_path, or to read the default.

    Call jme_ephemeris_path()
    Result

    Returns the text. When you pass buffer, the text is written there and the return points at that buffer.

    jme_set_ephemeris_path

    What it does Sets the directory used to resolve a relative kernel name from jme_set_jpl_file(). Changing it closes any open kernel.

    When to use it Call it at startup when the kernel file does not sit on the default path.

    Where it fits Before a JPL call that reads a kernel file.

    Call jme_set_ephemeris_path(path)
    Arguments
    • path Filesystem path. For a kernel this is the .bsp file or the directory that holds it.
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_fixstar

    What it does Computes a named fixed star at Terrestrial Time.

    When to use it Use this when you have TT and a catalogue name.

    Where it fits Star longitudes on a chart. The UT form is jme_fixstar_ut.

    Call jme_fixstar(star, jd_et, flags, results, error)
    Arguments
    • star Star name in the fixed-star catalogue.
    • jd_et Terrestrial Time (TT) as a Julian date.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • results Caller-owned output array. Allocate it before the call.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_fixstar_ut

    What it does Computes a named fixed star at Universal Time.

    When to use it Use this when the clock is UT.

    Where it fits The usual star position. Magnitude alone is jme_fixstar_mag.

    Call jme_fixstar_ut(star, jd_ut, flags, results, error)
    Arguments
    • star Star name in the fixed-star catalogue.
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • results Caller-owned output array. Allocate it before the call.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_fixstar_mag

    What it does Looks up the visual magnitude of a named star.

    When to use it Use this when you need brightness and not a position.

    Where it fits A star list. It does not depend on the date.

    Call jme_fixstar_mag(star, mag, error)
    Arguments
    • star Star name in the fixed-star catalogue.
    • mag Receives the visual magnitude.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_fixstar2

    What it does Computes a named fixed star at Terrestrial Time, using the longer star-name interface.

    When to use it Use this when the catalogue key does not fit the shorter star argument.

    Where it fits Same result family as jme_fixstar. Prefer it for long traditional names.

    Call jme_fixstar2(star, jd_et, flags, results, error)
    Arguments
    • star Star name in the fixed-star catalogue.
    • jd_et Terrestrial Time (TT) as a Julian date.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • results Caller-owned output array. Allocate it before the call.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_fixstar2_ut

    What it does Computes a named fixed star at Universal Time, using the longer star-name interface.

    When to use it Use this when the clock is UT and the name is long.

    Where it fits The UT pair of jme_fixstar2.

    Call jme_fixstar2_ut(star, jd_ut, flags, results, error)
    Arguments
    • star Star name in the fixed-star catalogue.
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • results Caller-owned output array. Allocate it before the call.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_fixstar2_mag

    What it does Looks up magnitude through the longer star-name interface.

    When to use it Use this for a long catalogue key when you only need brightness.

    Where it fits A star list, with no date.

    Call jme_fixstar2_mag(star, mag, error)
    Arguments
    • star Star name in the fixed-star catalogue.
    • mag Receives the visual magnitude.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_library_path

    What it does Returns the filesystem path of the loaded library, when the platform provides it.

    When to use it Use this in a diagnostic when several builds are installed and you need to see which file ran.

    Where it fits A support screen, not a calculation.

    Call jme_library_path()
    Result

    Returns the literal library identifier "jme". It is not a filesystem path.

    Function group

    General Utilities

    Use these for nodes and apsides, a distance range, or a small Julian-date adjustment that is not a body position.

    jme_nod_aps

    What it does Computes the times of the nodes and apsides of a body at a Terrestrial Time epoch.

    When to use it Use this when you need ascending node, descending node, perihelion, and aphelion near a TT date.

    Where it fits Orbital geometry. method selects the algorithm.

    Call jme_nod_aps(jd_et, body, flags, method, tret, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_et Terrestrial Time (TT) as a Julian date.
    • body Body id such as JME_BODY_SUN. The body constants list every id.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • method Algorithm selector for nodes and apsides. Use the method values documented for this call.
    • tret Caller-owned array of Julian dates. The description says which index is which event.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_nod_aps_ut

    What it does Computes nodes and apsides starting from Universal Time.

    When to use it Use this when the epoch clock is UT.

    Where it fits The UT pair of jme_nod_aps.

    Call jme_nod_aps_ut(jd_ut, body, flags, method, tret, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • body Body id such as JME_BODY_SUN. The body constants list every id.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • method Algorithm selector for nodes and apsides. Use the method values documented for this call.
    • tret Caller-owned array of Julian dates. The description says which index is which event.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_orbit_max_min_true_distance

    What it does Finds the nearby times and values of maximum and minimum true distance.

    When to use it Use this when the question is how near and how far the body gets around this date.

    Where it fits Distance ranges. Outputs are tmax, tmin, dmax, and dmin.

    Call jme_orbit_max_min_true_distance(jd_et, body, flags, tmax, tmin, dmax, dmin, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_et Terrestrial Time (TT) as a Julian date.
    • body Body id such as JME_BODY_SUN. The body constants list every id.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • tmax Receives the time of maximum true distance.
    • tmin Receives the time of minimum true distance.
    • dmax Receives the maximum true distance.
    • dmin Receives the minimum true distance.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_double_to_long

    What it does Rounds a floating-point number to the nearest integer.

    When to use it Use this for a display count, not for a longitude you will compute with again.

    Where it fits Halfway cases move away from zero.

    Call jme_double_to_long(x)
    Arguments
    • x Number to round to the nearest integer, away from zero on a tie.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_jd_add_seconds

    What it does Adds a number of seconds to a Julian date.

    When to use it Use this to step a search or to apply a small clock correction without rebuilding the calendar date.

    Where it fits The result is another Julian date.

    Call jme_jd_add_seconds(jd, seconds)
    Arguments
    • jd Julian date. The description of the call says which time scale that number is.
    • seconds A number of seconds to add, or the seconds field of a clock time.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    Function group

    Houses and Topocentric Geometry

    Use these for a chart on Earth: the observer, the house cusps, and which house a longitude falls in. Set the place before a topocentric planet.

    jme_set_topo

    What it does Stores the observer longitude, latitude, and height for later topocentric calls.

    When to use it Call it before any position, house, or rise that should be for a place rather than the geocentre.

    Where it fits Once per observer. The checked form rejects a latitude outside -90 to 90.

    Call jme_set_topo(lon, lat, altitude)
    Arguments
    • lon Geographic longitude in degrees. East is positive. The checked setter wraps it into the half-open range around zero.
    • lat Geographic latitude in degrees. The checked setter rejects a value outside -90 to 90.
    • altitude Observer height in metres.
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_houses

    What it does Computes the twelve house cusps and the angles for a place at Universal Time.

    When to use it Use this for a natal or horary chart when you do not need cusp speeds or extra flags.

    Where it fits After you know UT, latitude, and longitude. Pick the system with a JME_HOUSE_* id.

    Call jme_houses(jd_ut, geo_lat, geo_lon, house_system, cusps, ascmc)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time of the chart, as a Julian date.
    • geo_lat Geographic latitude in degrees. North is positive.
    • geo_lon Geographic longitude in degrees. East is positive.
    • house_system House-system id such as JME_HOUSE_PLACIDUS. Do not pass JME_HOUSE_GAUQUELIN to the 12-cusp calls.
    • cusps Caller-owned cusp array. Twelve-cusp calls use 13 numbers (index 1 to 12). Gauquelin calls use 37 numbers.
    • ascmc Caller-owned array for the Ascendant, Midheaven, and the other angles this call returns.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_houses_ex

    What it does Computes house cusps with calculation flags such as sidereal or no nutation.

    When to use it Use this when the houses must follow the same sidereal mode or nutation choice as the planets.

    Where it fits A sidereal chart. Flags match the house flags documented for this call.

    Call jme_houses_ex(jd_ut, flags, geo_lat, geo_lon, house_system, cusps, ascmc)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • geo_lat Geographic latitude in degrees. North is positive.
    • geo_lon Geographic longitude in degrees. East is positive.
    • house_system House-system id such as JME_HOUSE_PLACIDUS. Do not pass JME_HOUSE_GAUQUELIN to the 12-cusp calls.
    • cusps Caller-owned cusp array. Twelve-cusp calls use 13 numbers (index 1 to 12). Gauquelin calls use 37 numbers.
    • ascmc Caller-owned array for the Ascendant, Midheaven, and the other angles this call returns.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_houses_ex2

    What it does Computes house cusps and the speed of each cusp and angle.

    When to use it Use this when a chart needs how fast the cusps are moving.

    Where it fits The same place and time as jme_houses_ex, with two more output arrays.

    Call jme_houses_ex2(jd_ut, flags, geo_lat, geo_lon, house_system, cusps, ascmc, cusps_speed, ascmc_speed)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • geo_lat Geographic latitude in degrees. North is positive.
    • geo_lon Geographic longitude in degrees. East is positive.
    • house_system House-system id such as JME_HOUSE_PLACIDUS. Do not pass JME_HOUSE_GAUQUELIN to the 12-cusp calls.
    • cusps Caller-owned cusp array. Twelve-cusp calls use 13 numbers (index 1 to 12). Gauquelin calls use 37 numbers.
    • ascmc Caller-owned array for the Ascendant, Midheaven, and the other angles this call returns.
    • cusps_speed Caller-owned array for the rate of each cusp. Use the same length as cusps.
    • ascmc_speed Caller-owned array for the rate of each angle in ascmc.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_houses_armc

    What it does Computes house cusps from the right ascension of the Midheaven and the obliquity.

    When to use it Use this when you already have RAMC and obliquity and you do not want the call to derive them from UT.

    Where it fits A house routine downstream of your own sidereal time.

    Call jme_houses_armc(armc, geo_lat, eps, house_system, cusps, ascmc)
    Arguments
    • armc Right ascension of the Midheaven, in degrees.
    • geo_lat Geographic latitude in degrees. North is positive.
    • eps Obliquity of the ecliptic, in degrees, at the date you are using.
    • house_system House-system id such as JME_HOUSE_PLACIDUS. Do not pass JME_HOUSE_GAUQUELIN to the 12-cusp calls.
    • cusps Caller-owned cusp array. Twelve-cusp calls use 13 numbers (index 1 to 12). Gauquelin calls use 37 numbers.
    • ascmc Caller-owned array for the Ascendant, Midheaven, and the other angles this call returns.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_houses_armc_ex2

    What it does Computes house cusps and their speeds from RAMC and obliquity.

    When to use it Use this when you have RAMC and you also need cusp rates.

    Where it fits The speed-aware pair of jme_houses_armc.

    Call jme_houses_armc_ex2(armc, geo_lat, eps, house_system, cusps, ascmc, cusps_speed, ascmc_speed)
    Arguments
    • armc Right ascension of the Midheaven, in degrees.
    • geo_lat Geographic latitude in degrees. North is positive.
    • eps Obliquity of the ecliptic, in degrees, at the date you are using.
    • house_system House-system id such as JME_HOUSE_PLACIDUS. Do not pass JME_HOUSE_GAUQUELIN to the 12-cusp calls.
    • cusps Caller-owned cusp array. Twelve-cusp calls use 13 numbers (index 1 to 12). Gauquelin calls use 37 numbers.
    • ascmc Caller-owned array for the Ascendant, Midheaven, and the other angles this call returns.
    • cusps_speed Caller-owned array for the rate of each cusp. Use the same length as cusps.
    • ascmc_speed Caller-owned array for the rate of each angle in ascmc.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_house_pos

    What it does Returns the house number, with a fraction, of one ecliptic longitude.

    When to use it Use this after the cusps exist and you want 'which house is this planet in'.

    Where it fits Per body, once the angles are known. xpin[0] is the longitude. A missing system returns a non-finite value.

    Call jme_house_pos(armc, geo_lat, eps, house_system, xpin, error)
    Arguments
    • armc Right ascension of the Midheaven, in degrees.
    • geo_lat Geographic latitude in degrees. North is positive.
    • eps Obliquity of the ecliptic, in degrees, at the date you are using.
    • house_system House-system id such as JME_HOUSE_PLACIDUS. Do not pass JME_HOUSE_GAUQUELIN to the 12-cusp calls.
    • xpin Ecliptic longitude of the point, in degrees, in the first element.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns the house position as a number such as 1.25 for a point a quarter of the way through house 1. Returns a non-finite value, and writes error, when the house system is unavailable.

    jme_gauquelin_sector

    What it does Computes the Gauquelin sector of one body or star for an observer.

    When to use it Use this when you need the sector number of a single body, not the whole cusp list.

    Where it fits After the observer place is known. imeth selects the sector method.

    Call jme_gauquelin_sector(jd_ut, body, starname, flags, imeth, geopos, atpress, attemp, dgsect, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • body Body id such as JME_BODY_SUN. The body constants list every id.
    • starname Star name. Use an empty string when the call is for a solar-system body.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • imeth Gauquelin method selector for the sector division.
    • geopos Observer longitude, latitude, and height, in that order, in degrees and metres.
    • atpress Atmospheric pressure at the observer, in millibars.
    • attemp Atmospheric temperature at the observer, in degrees Celsius.
    • dgsect Receives the Gauquelin sector number.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_get_topo_pos

    What it does Returns the observer position in astronomical units at Terrestrial Time.

    When to use it Use this when a topocentric vector must start from the stored observer.

    Where it fits After jme_set_topo. Polar motion is applied only when that option is on.

    Call jme_get_topo_pos(jd_et, pos_au, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_et Terrestrial Time (TT) as a Julian date.
    • pos_au Receives the observer position in astronomical units.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_equatorial_to_horizontal

    What it does Converts hour angle and declination to azimuth and altitude.

    When to use it Use this for a sky position at a known latitude: is the body up, and where.

    Where it fits After you have the hour angle. Refraction is separate, in jme_refract.

    Call jme_equatorial_to_horizontal(hour_angle, dec, geo_lat, azimuth, altitude)
    Arguments
    • hour_angle Hour angle in degrees, or the variable that receives it.
    • dec Declination in degrees, or the variable that receives it.
    • geo_lat Geographic latitude in degrees. North is positive.
    • azimuth Receives azimuth.
    • altitude Height. For an observer this is metres. For refraction this is the altitude angle in degrees.
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_horizontal_to_equatorial

    What it does Converts azimuth and altitude to hour angle and declination.

    When to use it Use this when the observation is a horizon reading and you need the equator.

    Where it fits You supply the observer latitude.

    Call jme_horizontal_to_equatorial(azimuth, altitude, geo_lat, hour_angle, dec)
    Arguments
    • azimuth Receives azimuth.
    • altitude Height. For an observer this is metres. For refraction this is the altitude angle in degrees.
    • geo_lat Geographic latitude in degrees. North is positive.
    • hour_angle Hour angle in degrees, or the variable that receives it.
    • dec Declination in degrees, or the variable that receives it.
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_house_system_name

    What it does Returns the display name of a house-system id.

    When to use it Use this to label a JME_HOUSE_* value in a menu.

    Where it fits Gauquelin sectors are computed by jme_houses_gauquelin, not by passing that id to jme_houses.

    Call jme_house_system_name(house_system)
    Arguments
    • house_system House-system id such as JME_HOUSE_PLACIDUS. Do not pass JME_HOUSE_GAUQUELIN to the 12-cusp calls.
    Result

    Returns a pointer to a static display name, or NULL for an unknown id.

    Function group

    JPL and CALCEPH Kernels

    Use these only when you read a .bsp kernel yourself. Open the file first. The date is the kernel's own time scale, not Universal Time, except for the calls whose names say utc.

    jme_jpl_file

    What it does Returns the kernel path currently selected for the high-level engine.

    When to use it Call it to confirm which file ENGINE=JPL will open.

    Where it fits After jme_set_jpl_file.

    Call jme_jpl_file()
    Result

    Returns the text. When you pass buffer, the text is written there and the return points at that buffer.

    jme_set_jpl_file

    What it does Selects the .bsp file used by the high-level JPL engine. The kernel is opened lazily on the next high-level calculation.

    When to use it Call it when ENGINE=JPL or ENGINE=AUTO should read a kernel.

    Where it fits Startup, before jme_calc. Low-level reads use jme_jpl_open instead.

    Call jme_set_jpl_file(path)
    Arguments
    • path Filesystem path to a .bsp file, or a relative kernel name resolved against jme_set_ephemeris_path().
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_jpl_body_state

    What it does Reads the position and velocity from the open kernel at one Julian date on the kernel's native time scale (TDB or TCB), identified by JME body ids. unit selects AU or kilometres, and per day or per second.

    When to use it Use this low-level read when you have one Julian date already expressed on the kernel time scale and you want the kernel vector rather than the ecliptic place from jme_calc.

    Where it fits After jme_jpl_open. Do not pass UT here. For a civil clock and an ecliptic longitude, use jme_calc_ut.

    Call jme_jpl_body_state(jd_time, target_body, center_body, unit, state, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_time Input or output for this call. The name is the shared argument name.
    • target_body Body id of the object you want.
    • center_body Body id of the origin of the vector. The solar-system barycentre and the Earth are both valid centers when the kernel has them.
    • unit Output unit. Position calls use a JME_VECTOR_* id. Orientation calls use a JME_ORIENTATION_* id.
    • state Caller-owned state array. Position calls use six numbers: position, then velocity.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_jpl_body_state_split

    What it does Reads the position and velocity from the open kernel at a split Julian date (jd0 + time_offset) on the kernel's native time scale, identified by JME body ids. unit selects AU or kilometres, and per day or per second.

    When to use it Use this low-level read when you already hold a split Julian date and need to keep that split and you want the kernel vector rather than the ecliptic place from jme_calc.

    Where it fits After jme_jpl_open. Do not pass UT here. For a civil clock and an ecliptic longitude, use jme_calc_ut.

    Call jme_jpl_body_state_split(jd0, time_offset, target_body, center_body, unit, state, error)
    Arguments
    • jd0 Coarse part of a split Julian date on the kernel time scale.
    • time_offset Small part added to jd0, so the split date keeps its digits.
    • target_body Body id of the object you want.
    • center_body Body id of the origin of the vector. The solar-system barycentre and the Earth are both valid centers when the kernel has them.
    • unit Output unit. Position calls use a JME_VECTOR_* id. Orientation calls use a JME_ORIENTATION_* id.
    • state Caller-owned state array. Position calls use six numbers: position, then velocity.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_jpl_ecliptic_state

    What it does Reads the ecliptic position and velocity from the open kernel at one Julian date on the kernel's native time scale (TDB or TCB), identified by JME body ids. unit selects AU or kilometres, and per day or per second.

    When to use it Use this low-level read when you have one Julian date already expressed on the kernel time scale and you want the kernel vector rather than the ecliptic place from jme_calc.

    Where it fits After jme_jpl_open. Do not pass UT here. For a civil clock and an ecliptic longitude, use jme_calc_ut.

    Call jme_jpl_ecliptic_state(jd_time, target_body, center_body, unit, state, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_time Input or output for this call. The name is the shared argument name.
    • target_body Body id of the object you want.
    • center_body Body id of the origin of the vector. The solar-system barycentre and the Earth are both valid centers when the kernel has them.
    • unit Output unit. Position calls use a JME_VECTOR_* id. Orientation calls use a JME_ORIENTATION_* id.
    • state Caller-owned state array. Position calls use six numbers: position, then velocity.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_jpl_body_state_naif

    What it does Reads the position and velocity from the open kernel at one Julian date on the kernel's native time scale (TDB or TCB), identified by NAIF ids. unit selects AU or kilometres, and per day or per second.

    When to use it Use this low-level read when you have one Julian date already expressed on the kernel time scale and you want the kernel vector rather than the ecliptic place from jme_calc.

    Where it fits After jme_jpl_open. Do not pass UT here. For a civil clock and an ecliptic longitude, use jme_calc_ut.

    jme_jpl_body_state_utc_naif

    What it does Reads the position and velocity from the open kernel at a UTC calendar date, converted inside the call onto the kernel time scale, identified by NAIF ids. unit selects AU or kilometres, and per day or per second.

    When to use it Use this low-level read when the time you have is a UTC calendar date and you want the kernel vector rather than the ecliptic place from jme_calc.

    Where it fits After jme_jpl_open. Do not pass UT here. For a civil clock and an ecliptic longitude, use jme_calc_ut.

    Call jme_jpl_body_state_utc_naif(year, month, day, hour, minute, second, calendar, target_naif, center_naif, unit, state, error)
    Arguments
    • year Calendar year. Astronomical year numbering, so 1 BCE is year 0.
    • month Month number from 1 to 12.
    • day Day of the month.
    • hour Hour. Where the call takes a decimal hour, fractions of an hour are allowed.
    • minute Minute.
    • second Second, including the fraction. A leap second 60 is accepted only on a UTC path that validates it.
    • calendar JME_CALENDAR_GREGORIAN or JME_CALENDAR_JULIAN.
    • target_naif NAIF id of the object, as stored in the kernel.
    • center_naif NAIF id of the origin of the vector.
    • unit Output unit. Position calls use a JME_VECTOR_* id. Orientation calls use a JME_ORIENTATION_* id.
    • state Caller-owned state array. Position calls use six numbers: position, then velocity.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_jpl_close

    What it does Closes the kernel opened for the low-level JPL calls.

    When to use it Call it when you are finished with jme_jpl_body_state and the other kernel reads.

    Where it fits The high-level engine has its own file selection through jme_set_jpl_file.

    Call jme_jpl_close()
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_jpl_coverage

    What it does Reports the first time, last time, and whether the open kernel coverage is continuous.

    When to use it Call it before a date that might fall outside the file.

    Where it fits After jme_jpl_open.

    Call jme_jpl_coverage(first_time, last_time, continuous, error)
    Arguments
    • first_time Receives the first time the kernel covers.
    • last_time Receives the last time the kernel covers.
    • continuous Receives non-zero when the coverage has no gap.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_jpl_constant

    What it does Reads one numeric constant from the open kernel by name.

    When to use it Use this for a kernel header value such as a defined constant the file publishes.

    Where it fits After the kernel is open. The name is the kernel's own constant name.

    Call jme_jpl_constant(name, value, error)
    Arguments
    • name Name to look up, or the buffer that receives a name.
    • value Receives one numeric kernel constant.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_jpl_constant_count

    What it does Returns how many constants the open kernel publishes.

    When to use it Use this before you loop with jme_jpl_constant_index.

    Where it fits A kernel inspection screen.

    Call jme_jpl_constant_count(error)
    Arguments
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_jpl_constant_index

    What it does Reads one kernel constant by its index, returning the name and the value.

    When to use it Use this to list every constant when you do not know the names.

    Where it fits Index runs from zero to one less than jme_jpl_constant_count.

    Call jme_jpl_constant_index(index, name, name_size, value, error)
    Arguments
    • index Zero-based index into the kernel list you are reading.
    • name Name to look up, or the buffer that receives a name.
    • name_size Size of the name buffer, in bytes.
    • value Receives one numeric kernel constant.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_jpl_constant_vector

    What it does Reads a numeric kernel constant that has several values.

    When to use it Use this when jme_jpl_constant is the wrong shape because the constant is a vector.

    Where it fits value_count is how many numbers you allocated.

    Call jme_jpl_constant_vector(name, values, value_count, error)
    Arguments
    • name Name to look up, or the buffer that receives a name.
    • values Receives several numeric kernel constants, or the text buffer for a string vector.
    • value_count How many values to write.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_jpl_constant_string

    What it does Reads a text kernel constant by name.

    When to use it Use this for a kernel constant that is a string rather than a number.

    Where it fits value is your buffer.

    Call jme_jpl_constant_string(name, value, value_size, error)
    Arguments
    • name Name to look up, or the buffer that receives a name.
    • value Receives one numeric kernel constant.
    • value_size Size of one text value, in bytes.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_jpl_constant_string_vector

    What it does Reads a kernel constant that is a list of strings.

    When to use it Use this when the constant is several text values.

    Where it fits Each slot is single_value_size bytes.

    Call jme_jpl_constant_string_vector(name, values, single_value_size, value_count, error)
    Arguments
    • name Name to look up, or the buffer that receives a name.
    • values Receives several numeric kernel constants, or the text buffer for a string vector.
    • single_value_size Size of each text slot in the string vector.
    • value_count How many values to write.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_jpl_engine_version

    What it does Copies the CALCEPH build version into buffer.

    When to use it Call it in a diagnostic next to jme_version, so you can see the kernel library as well as JME.

    Where it fits It does not need a kernel to be open.

    Call jme_jpl_engine_version(buffer, buffer_size)
    Arguments
    • buffer Caller-owned character buffer. The call writes the text here.
    • buffer_size Size of buffer, in bytes, including room for the terminating zero.
    Result

    Returns the text. When you pass buffer, the text is written there and the return points at that buffer.
