    Where it fits After jme_jpl_open.

    Call jme_jpl_file_version(buffer, buffer_size, error)
    Arguments
    • buffer Caller-owned character buffer. The call writes the text here.
    • buffer_size Size of buffer, in bytes, including room for the terminating zero.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_jpl_current_file_data

    What it does Reports the open kernel path and its coverage in one call.

    When to use it Use this on a status screen instead of calling path and coverage separately.

    Where it fits After jme_jpl_open.

    Call jme_jpl_current_file_data(path, path_size, first_time, last_time, continuous, error)
    Arguments
    • path Filesystem path. For a kernel this is the .bsp file or the directory that holds it.
    • path_size Size of the path buffer, in bytes.
    • first_time Receives the first time the kernel covers.
    • last_time Receives the last time the kernel covers.
    • continuous Receives non-zero when the coverage has no gap.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_jpl_is_available

    What it does Reports whether this build of JME was linked with CALCEPH.

    When to use it Call it before you offer a JPL mode. A build without CALCEPH cannot open a kernel.

    Where it fits Startup. The analytical engines still work when this returns false.

    Call jme_jpl_is_available()
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_jpl_is_open

    What it does Reports whether a kernel is currently open.

    When to use it Call it before a low-level state read.

    Where it fits After jme_jpl_open or jme_jpl_close.

    Call jme_jpl_is_open()
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_jpl_open

    What it does Opens one kernel file for the low-level JPL calls.

    When to use it Call it when you will use jme_jpl_body_state rather than jme_calc.

    Where it fits A planet-centre that lives in a second file needs jme_jpl_open_array.

    Call jme_jpl_open(path, error)
    Arguments
    • path Filesystem path. For a kernel this is the .bsp file or the directory that holds it.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_jpl_open_array

    What it does Opens several kernel files together.

    When to use it Use this for a planetary kernel plus the satellite kernels that hold planet centres.

    Where it fits paths lists the files. This is how you avoid substituting a system barycentre.

    Call jme_jpl_open_array(path_count, paths, error)
    Arguments
    • path_count How many kernel paths are in the list.
    • paths List of kernel paths to open together, for a planet kernel plus its satellite kernels.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_jpl_prefetch

    What it does Asks the kernel library to read ahead.

    When to use it Use this before a tight loop of state calls when you want the file cached.

    Where it fits After the kernel is open, before the loop.

    Call jme_jpl_prefetch(error)
    Arguments
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_jpl_is_thread_safe

    What it does Reports whether this CALCEPH build may be called from more than one thread.

    When to use it Call it before you share one open kernel across threads.

    Where it fits A negative answer means you keep the JPL calls on one thread.

    Call jme_jpl_is_thread_safe(error)
    Arguments
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_jpl_id_by_name

    What it does Looks up a kernel object id from its name.

    When to use it Use this when the user has a kernel name and the state call wants an id.

    Where it fits After the kernel is open.

    Call jme_jpl_id_by_name(name, id, error)
    Arguments
    • name Name to look up, or the buffer that receives a name.
    • id Receives a body or kernel id.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_jpl_name_by_id

    What it does Looks up a kernel object name from its id.

    When to use it Use this to label a NAIF id.

    Where it fits After the kernel is open.

    Call jme_jpl_name_by_id(id, name, name_size, error)
    Arguments
    • id Receives a body or kernel id.
    • name Name to look up, or the buffer that receives a name.
    • name_size Size of the name buffer, in bytes.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_jpl_max_supported_order

    What it does Returns the highest derivative order a kernel segment type can provide.

    When to use it Call it before jme_jpl_body_state_order when you might ask for a derivative the segment does not have.

    Where it fits segment_type comes from a record-index call.

    Call jme_jpl_max_supported_order(segment_type)
    Arguments
    • segment_type Kernel segment type, used to ask which derivative order that segment can return.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_jpl_position_record_count

    What it does Returns how many position records the open kernel contains.

    When to use it Use this before you loop with jme_jpl_position_record_index.

    Where it fits A kernel inventory.

    Call jme_jpl_position_record_count(error)
    Arguments
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_jpl_position_record_index

    What it does Reads one position record: target, centre, time span, frame, and segment type.

    When to use it Use this to see which bodies the file can actually compute.

    Where it fits Index runs from zero to one less than the record count.

    Call jme_jpl_position_record_index(index, target, center, first_time, last_time, frame, segment_type, error)
    Arguments
    • index Zero-based index into the kernel list you are reading.
    • target Receives the target id of one kernel record.
    • center Body id used as the origin instead of the default centre.
    • first_time Receives the first time the kernel covers.
    • last_time Receives the last time the kernel covers.
    • frame Receives the frame id of one kernel record.
    • segment_type Kernel segment type, used to ask which derivative order that segment can return.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_jpl_orientation_state_naif

    What it does Reads the orientation state from the open kernel at one Julian date on the kernel's native time scale (TDB or TCB), identified by NAIF ids. unit selects radians per day or radians per second.

    When to use it Use this low-level read when you have one Julian date already expressed on the kernel time scale and you want the kernel vector rather than the ecliptic place from jme_calc.

    Where it fits After jme_jpl_open. Do not pass UT here. For a civil clock and an ecliptic longitude, use jme_calc_ut.

    Call jme_jpl_orientation_state_naif(jd_time, target_naif, unit, state, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_time Input or output for this call. The name is the shared argument name.
    • target_naif NAIF id of the object, as stored in the kernel.
    • unit Output unit. Position calls use a JME_VECTOR_* id. Orientation calls use a JME_ORIENTATION_* id.
    • state Caller-owned state array. Position calls use six numbers: position, then velocity.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_jpl_orientation_state_split_naif

    What it does Reads the orientation state from the open kernel at a split Julian date (jd0 + time_offset) on the kernel's native time scale, identified by NAIF ids. unit selects radians per day or radians per second.

    When to use it Use this low-level read when you already hold a split Julian date and need to keep that split and you want the kernel vector rather than the ecliptic place from jme_calc.

    Where it fits After jme_jpl_open. Do not pass UT here. For a civil clock and an ecliptic longitude, use jme_calc_ut.

    Call jme_jpl_orientation_state_split_naif(jd0, time_offset, target_naif, unit, state, error)
    Arguments
    • jd0 Coarse part of a split Julian date on the kernel time scale.
    • time_offset Small part added to jd0, so the split date keeps its digits.
    • target_naif NAIF id of the object, as stored in the kernel.
    • unit Output unit. Position calls use a JME_VECTOR_* id. Orientation calls use a JME_ORIENTATION_* id.
    • state Caller-owned state array. Position calls use six numbers: position, then velocity.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_jpl_orientation_state_order_naif

    What it does Reads the orientation state from the open kernel at a split Julian date (jd0 + time_offset) on the kernel's native time scale, identified by NAIF ids. order asks for derivatives beyond velocity. unit selects radians per day or radians per second.

    When to use it Use this low-level read when you already hold a split Julian date and need to keep that split and you want the kernel vector rather than the ecliptic place from jme_calc.

    Where it fits After jme_jpl_open. Do not pass UT here. For a civil clock and an ecliptic longitude, use jme_calc_ut.

    Call jme_jpl_orientation_state_order_naif(jd0, time_offset, target_naif, unit, order, state, error)
    Arguments
    • jd0 Coarse part of a split Julian date on the kernel time scale.
    • time_offset Small part added to jd0, so the split date keeps its digits.
    • target_naif NAIF id of the object, as stored in the kernel.
    • unit Output unit. Position calls use a JME_VECTOR_* id. Orientation calls use a JME_ORIENTATION_* id.
    • order Highest derivative to return. Zero is position only.
    • state Caller-owned state array. Position calls use six numbers: position, then velocity.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_jpl_orientation_state_utc_naif

    What it does Reads the orientation state from the open kernel at a UTC calendar date, converted inside the call onto the kernel time scale, identified by NAIF ids. unit selects radians per day or radians per second.

    When to use it Use this low-level read when the time you have is a UTC calendar date and you want the kernel vector rather than the ecliptic place from jme_calc.

    Where it fits After jme_jpl_open. Do not pass UT here. For a civil clock and an ecliptic longitude, use jme_calc_ut.

    Call jme_jpl_orientation_state_utc_naif(year, month, day, hour, minute, second, calendar, target_naif, unit, state, error)
    Arguments
    • year Calendar year. Astronomical year numbering, so 1 BCE is year 0.
    • month Month number from 1 to 12.
    • day Day of the month.
    • hour Hour. Where the call takes a decimal hour, fractions of an hour are allowed.
    • minute Minute.
    • second Second, including the fraction. A leap second 60 is accepted only on a UTC path that validates it.
    • calendar JME_CALENDAR_GREGORIAN or JME_CALENDAR_JULIAN.
    • target_naif NAIF id of the object, as stored in the kernel.
    • unit Output unit. Position calls use a JME_VECTOR_* id. Orientation calls use a JME_ORIENTATION_* id.
    • state Caller-owned state array. Position calls use six numbers: position, then velocity.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    • state Caller-owned state array. Position calls use six numbers: position, then velocity.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    jme_jpl_orientation_record_count

    What it does Returns how many orientation records the open kernel contains.

    When to use it Use this before an orientation loop. Many planetary kernels have none.

    Where it fits A kernel inventory.

    Call jme_jpl_orientation_record_count(error)
    Arguments
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.

    jme_jpl_orientation_record_index

    What it does Reads one orientation record: target, time span, frame, and segment type.

    When to use it Use this to see whether a body has an orientation series.

    Where it fits Index runs from zero to one less than the orientation record count.

    Call jme_jpl_orientation_record_index(index, target, first_time, last_time, frame, segment_type, error)
    Arguments
    • index Zero-based index into the kernel list you are reading.
    • target Receives the target id of one kernel record.
    • first_time Receives the first time the kernel covers.
    • last_time Receives the last time the kernel covers.
