    jme_jpl_timescale

    What it does Returns the native time scale of the open kernel, TDB or TCB.

    When to use it Call it before a low-level state call so you pass a date on that scale.

    Where it fits High-level jme_calc converts TT for you. These low-level calls do not.

    Call jme_jpl_timescale()
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    Function group

    Main Body Calculations

    Start here for a Sun, Moon, planet, or node. jme_calc_ut is the usual call from a civil clock. The other calls in this group are appearance, names, or one chosen analytical series.

    jme_calc

    What it does Computes a body position at Terrestrial Time.

    When to use it Use this when the instant you have is already TT. For a civil clock, use jme_calc_ut.

    Where it fits The usual planet, Sun, Moon, or node position. flags choose equatorial, rectangular, topocentric, sidereal, and the other frames.

    Call jme_calc(jd_et, body, flags, results, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_et Terrestrial Time (TT) as a Julian date.
    • body Body id such as JME_BODY_SUN. The body constants list every id.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • results Six numbers you allocate. Indexes 0–2 are position. Indexes 3–5 are the rates. The call fills the rates even when JME_CALC_SPEED is absent.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK or JME_ERR. On JME_OK, results holds six numbers: position in 0–2 and rates in 3–5.

    jme_calc_ut

    What it does Computes a body position at Universal Time.

    When to use it Use this when the instant you have is UT, including a Julian date built from a civil clock.

    Where it fits The usual entry for a chart or a panchang. The six results are position then rates.

    Call jme_calc_ut(jd_ut, body, flags, results, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • body Body id such as JME_BODY_SUN. The body constants list every id.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • results Six numbers you allocate. Indexes 0–2 are position. Indexes 3–5 are the rates. The call fills the rates even when JME_CALC_SPEED is absent.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK or JME_ERR. On JME_OK, results holds six numbers: position in 0–2 and rates in 3–5.

    jme_calc_pctr

    What it does Computes a body position relative to an explicit centre, at Terrestrial Time.

    When to use it Use this when the origin must be a chosen body, not the default geocentric or heliocentric centre.

    Where it fits Relative positions, such as a moon of a planet seen from that planet, at TT.

    Call jme_calc_pctr(jd_et, body, center, flags, results, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_et Terrestrial Time (TT) as a Julian date.
    • body Body id such as JME_BODY_SUN. The body constants list every id.
    • center Body id used as the origin instead of the default centre.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • results Six numbers you allocate, same layout as jme_calc: position, then rates, relative to center.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK or JME_ERR. On JME_OK, results holds six numbers: position in 0–2 and rates in 3–5.

    jme_pheno

    What it does Computes appearance data for a body at Terrestrial Time, such as phase and elongation.

    When to use it Use this when you need how the body looks, not its ecliptic longitude.

    Where it fits After you already know the body and the TT date. The UT form is jme_pheno_ut.

    Call jme_pheno(jd_et, body, flags, attr, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_et Terrestrial Time (TT) as a Julian date.
    • body Body id such as JME_BODY_SUN. The body constants list every id.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • attr Caller-owned array that receives the circumstance values for this call.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_pheno_ut

    What it does Computes appearance data for a body at Universal Time.

    When to use it Use this when the clock is UT and you need phase, elongation, and the related attributes.

    Where it fits A planet panel or a lunar-phase display. For the longitude itself, use jme_calc_ut.

    Call jme_pheno_ut(jd_ut, body, flags, attr, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • body Body id such as JME_BODY_SUN. The body constants list every id.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • attr Caller-owned array that receives the circumstance values for this call.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_heliacal_pheno_ut

    What it does Computes the heliacal appearance attributes at a known Universal Time.

    When to use it Use this when the time is already chosen and you need the visibility circumstances.

    Where it fits The attribute pair of the heliacal search.

    Call jme_heliacal_pheno_ut(jd_ut, geopos, dat_hel, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • geopos Observer longitude, latitude, and height, in that order, in degrees and metres.
    • dat_hel Caller-owned array of the shared heliacal inputs: place, atmosphere, and object data.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_matrix_transform_state

    What it does Applies a 3 by 3 matrix to a Cartesian state.

    When to use it Use this after you have built a precession or nutation matrix and you still hold x, y, z and their rates.

    Where it fits input and output are states. output is caller-owned.

    Call jme_matrix_transform_state(m, input, output)
    Arguments
    • m Caller-owned rotation matrix, nine numbers, row by row.
    • input State or matrix going in.
    • output Caller-owned state or matrix coming out.
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_body_id_from_name

    What it does Returns the body id for a name such as Sun or Moon.

    When to use it Use this when a user typed a name and the calculation calls want an id.

    Where it fits A name that is not a body returns an id you should test before jme_calc.

    Call jme_body_id_from_name(name)
    Arguments
    • name Name to look up, or the buffer that receives a name.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_body_name

    What it does Returns the library's name for a body id.

    When to use it Use this to label a JME_BODY_* value.

    Where it fits The pointer is library-owned text. Copy it if you need to keep it.

    Call jme_body_name(body)
    Arguments
    • body Body id such as JME_BODY_SUN. The body constants list every id.
    Result

    Returns library-owned text. Generated names for Asteroid 013..110, Comet 001..060, and Minor Planet 001..060 use a thread-local buffer, overwritten by the next generated body name returned on the same thread. Copy the text if you need to keep it.

    jme_copy_body_name

    What it does Copies a body name into your buffer.

    When to use it Use this when the binding must own the string.

    Where it fits Safer than holding the pointer from jme_body_name across later calls.

    Call jme_copy_body_name(body, buffer)
    Arguments
    • body Body id such as JME_BODY_SUN. The body constants list every id.
    • buffer Caller-owned character buffer. The call writes the text here.
    Result

    Returns the text. When you pass buffer, the text is written there and the return points at that buffer.

    jme_body_naif_id

    What it does Returns the NAIF id that corresponds to a JME body id.

    When to use it Use this before a jme_jpl_*_naif call when you started from JME_BODY_*.

    Where it fits Kernel code. The reverse lookup is jme_jpl_name_by_id.

    Call jme_body_naif_id(body)
    Arguments
    • body Body id such as JME_BODY_SUN. The body constants list every id.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_ecliptic_to_equatorial_rectangular_state

    What it does Rotates an ecliptic Cartesian state onto the equator.

    When to use it Use this when you hold x, y, z and their rates, not spherical angles.

    Where it fits eps is the obliquity. The reverse is the equatorial-to-ecliptic state call.

    Call jme_ecliptic_to_equatorial_rectangular_state(ecliptic, eps, equatorial)
    Arguments
    • ecliptic Ecliptic rectangular state.
    • eps Obliquity of the ecliptic, in degrees, at the date you are using.
    • equatorial Equatorial rectangular state.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_equatorial_to_ecliptic_rectangular_state

    What it does Rotates an equatorial Cartesian state onto the ecliptic.

    When to use it Use this for a rectangular state that must be expressed in ecliptic axes.

    Where it fits The reverse of the ecliptic-to-equatorial state call.

    Call jme_equatorial_to_ecliptic_rectangular_state(equatorial, eps, ecliptic)
    Arguments
    • equatorial Equatorial rectangular state.
    • eps Obliquity of the ecliptic, in degrees, at the date you are using.
    • ecliptic Ecliptic rectangular state.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_spherical_to_rectangular_state

    What it does Converts a spherical state to a rectangular state.

    When to use it Use this when a later kernel-style step wants x, y, z and rates.

    Where it fits The reverse is jme_rectangular_to_spherical_state.

    Call jme_spherical_to_rectangular_state(spherical, rectangular)
    Arguments
    • spherical Spherical state: longitude, latitude, distance, and their rates.
    • rectangular Rectangular state: x, y, z, and their rates.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_rectangular_to_spherical_state

    What it does Converts a rectangular state to longitude, latitude, distance, and their rates.

    When to use it Use this after a rectangular kernel read when you want spherical coordinates.

    Where it fits The reverse is jme_spherical_to_rectangular_state.

    Call jme_rectangular_to_spherical_state(rectangular, spherical)
    Arguments
    • rectangular Rectangular state: x, y, z, and their rates.
    • spherical Spherical state: longitude, latitude, distance, and their rates.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_state_distance

    What it does Returns the distance from the position part of a Cartesian state.

    When to use it Use this when you have x, y, z and need the range.

    Where it fits A state from jme_jpl_body_state or a rectangular conversion.

    Call jme_state_distance(state)
    Arguments
    • state Caller-owned state array. Position calls use six numbers: position, then velocity.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_state_convert_units

    What it does Converts a Cartesian state between AU and kilometres, and between per day and per second.

    When to use it Use this when a kernel vector must be shown in kilometres per second, or the reverse.

    Where it fits input_unit and output_unit are JME_VECTOR_* ids.

    Call jme_state_convert_units(input, input_unit, output_unit, output)
    Arguments
    • input State or matrix going in.
    • input_unit Unit of the input state, a JME_VECTOR_* id.
    • output_unit Unit wanted in the output state, a JME_VECTOR_* id.
    • output Caller-owned state or matrix coming out.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_state_light_time_days

    What it does Returns the light time of a state, in days.

    When to use it Use this when you need the light-time delay of a distance you already hold.

    Where it fits unit says whether the state is in AU or kilometres.

    Call jme_state_light_time_days(state, unit)
    Arguments
    • state Caller-owned state array. Position calls use six numbers: position, then velocity.
    • unit Output unit. Position calls use a JME_VECTOR_* id. Orientation calls use a JME_ORIENTATION_* id.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_state_position_velocity_dot

    What it does Returns the dot product of the position and velocity parts of a state.

    When to use it Use this in your own range-rate geometry.

    Where it fits A 6-number state.

    Call jme_state_position_velocity_dot(state)
    Arguments
    • state Caller-owned state array. Position calls use six numbers: position, then velocity.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_state_speed

    What it does Returns the speed from the velocity part of a state.

    When to use it Use this to show how fast the body is moving in the state's unit.

    Where it fits It does not recompute a position.

    Call jme_state_speed(state)
    Arguments
    • state Caller-owned state array. Position calls use six numbers: position, then velocity.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_state_add

    What it does Adds two Cartesian states.

    When to use it Use this to combine a barycentric vector with an offset you already have.

    Where it fits output is caller-owned.

    Call jme_state_add(left, right, output)
    Arguments
    • left First state in the sum or difference.
    • right Second state in the sum or difference.
    • output Caller-owned state or matrix coming out.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_state_scale

    What it does Multiplies every component of a state by a factor.

    When to use it Use this for a unit scale the conversion helper does not cover.

    Where it fits output is caller-owned.

    Call jme_state_scale(input, factor, output)
    Arguments
    • input State or matrix going in.
    • factor Number to multiply every component by.
    • output Caller-owned state or matrix coming out.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_state_subtract

    What it does Subtracts one Cartesian state from another.

    When to use it Use this to change the origin of a vector, when both states share a frame and a unit.

    Where it fits output is caller-owned.

    Call jme_state_subtract(left, right, output)
    Arguments
    • left First state in the sum or difference.
    • right Second state in the sum or difference.
    • output Caller-owned state or matrix coming out.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_vsop87_planet_state

    What it does Computes a planet with the VSOP87 series at Terrestrial Time.

    When to use it Use this only when you want VSOP87 specifically, not the engine selected by jme_set_astro_models.

    Where it fits A direct theory call. For the normal position, use jme_calc.

    Call jme_vsop87_planet_state(jd_et, body, results)
    Arguments
    • jd_et Terrestrial Time (TT) as a Julian date.
    • body Body id such as JME_BODY_SUN. The body constants list every id.
    • results Caller-owned output array. Allocate it before the call.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_meeus_sun_state

    What it does Computes the Sun with the Meeus series at Terrestrial Time.

    When to use it Use this when you want that solar series specifically.

    Where it fits A direct theory call. The engine switch does not apply.

    Call jme_meeus_sun_state(jd_et, results)
    Arguments
    • jd_et Terrestrial Time (TT) as a Julian date.
    • results Caller-owned output array. Allocate it before the call.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_meeus_moon_state

    What it does Computes the Moon with the Meeus series at Terrestrial Time.

    When to use it Use this when you want that lunar series specifically.

    Where it fits A direct theory call.

    Call jme_meeus_moon_state(jd_et, results)
    Arguments
    • jd_et Terrestrial Time (TT) as a Julian date.
    • results Caller-owned output array. Allocate it before the call.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_elp2000_moon_state

    What it does Computes the Moon with ELP2000-82B at Terrestrial Time.

    When to use it Use this when you want ELP specifically.

    Where it fits A direct theory call. The high-level engine can select this series for you.

    Call jme_elp2000_moon_state(jd_et, results)
    Arguments
    • jd_et Terrestrial Time (TT) as a Julian date.
    • results Caller-owned output array. Allocate it before the call.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_meeus_planet_state

    What it does Computes a planet with the Meeus planetary series at Terrestrial Time.

    When to use it Use this when you want that series specifically.

    Where it fits A direct theory call.

    Call jme_meeus_planet_state(jd_et, body, results)
    Arguments
    • jd_et Terrestrial Time (TT) as a Julian date.
    • body Body id such as JME_BODY_SUN. The body constants list every id.
    • results Caller-owned output array. Allocate it before the call.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_moshier_planet_state

    What it does Computes a body with the Moshier analytical theory at Terrestrial Time.

    When to use it Use this when you want Moshier specifically, including in a comparison against JPL.

    Where it fits A direct theory call. ENGINE=MOSHIER on jme_calc is the usual way to select it.

    Call jme_moshier_planet_state(jd_et, body, results)
    Arguments
    • jd_et Terrestrial Time (TT) as a Julian date.
    • body Body id such as JME_BODY_SUN. The body constants list every id.
    • results Caller-owned output array. Allocate it before the call.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    Function group

    Rise, Set, and Crossings

    Use these when the result you want is a time: a rise, a set, a transit, or the moment a longitude is reached. The start date is where the search begins.

    jme_rise_trans

    What it does Finds the next rise, set, or transit of a body or star at a place.

    When to use it Use this for the time the object crosses the horizon or the meridian.

    Where it fits A panchang sunrise, moonrise, or a planet rise. rsmi is a JME_RISE_* value. The UT date is the search start.

    Call jme_rise_trans(jd_ut, body, starname, flags, rsmi, geopos, atpress, attemp, tret, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • body Body id such as JME_BODY_SUN. The body constants list every id.
    • starname Star name. Use an empty string when the call is for a solar-system body.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • rsmi What to find: a JME_RISE_* value such as rise, set, transit, or a twilight.
    • geopos Observer longitude, latitude, and height, in that order, in degrees and metres.
    • atpress Atmospheric pressure at the observer, in millibars.
    • attemp Atmospheric temperature at the observer, in degrees Celsius.
    • tret Caller-owned array of Julian dates. The description says which index is which event.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_rise_trans_true_hor

    What it does Finds rise, set, or transit against a horizon you raise or lower.

    When to use it Use this when the local horizon is not the geometric one, for example a hill of known altitude.

    Where it fits Same inputs as jme_rise_trans, plus horhgt in degrees.

    Call jme_rise_trans_true_hor(jd_ut, body, starname, flags, rsmi, geopos, atpress, attemp, horhgt, tret, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • body Body id such as JME_BODY_SUN. The body constants list every id.
    • starname Star name. Use an empty string when the call is for a solar-system body.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • rsmi What to find: a JME_RISE_* value such as rise, set, transit, or a twilight.
    • geopos Observer longitude, latitude, and height, in that order, in degrees and metres.
    • atpress Atmospheric pressure at the observer, in millibars.
    • attemp Atmospheric temperature at the observer, in degrees Celsius.
    • horhgt Height of the local horizon above the geometric horizon, in degrees.
    • tret Caller-owned array of Julian dates. The description says which index is which event.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_solcross

    What it does Finds when the Sun next reaches an ecliptic longitude, on the Terrestrial Time entry.

    When to use it Use this when your start instant is TT.

    Where it fits Ingress and sankranti calculations. The UT entry is jme_solcross_ut.

    Call jme_solcross(x2cross, jd_ut, flags, tret, error)
    Arguments
    • x2cross Ecliptic longitude to reach, in degrees.
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • tret Caller-owned array of Julian dates. The description says which index is which event.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_solcross_ut

    What it does Finds when the Sun next reaches an ecliptic longitude, starting from Universal Time.

    When to use it Use this for a civil date and a target longitude such as 0° for the March equinox longitude.

    Where it fits A calendar of solar ingresses.

    Call jme_solcross_ut(x2cross, jd_ut, flags, tret, error)
    Arguments
    • x2cross Ecliptic longitude to reach, in degrees.
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • tret Caller-owned array of Julian dates. The description says which index is which event.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_mooncross

    What it does Finds when the Moon next reaches an ecliptic longitude, on the Terrestrial Time entry.

    When to use it Use this when the start instant is TT.

    Where it fits Tithi or nakshatra boundaries when you already hold TT.

    Call jme_mooncross(x2cross, jd_ut, flags, tret, error)
    Arguments
    • x2cross Ecliptic longitude to reach, in degrees.
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • tret Caller-owned array of Julian dates. The description says which index is which event.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_mooncross_ut

    What it does Finds when the Moon next reaches an ecliptic longitude, starting from Universal Time.

    When to use it Use this for rashi, nakshatra, or tithi edges from a civil clock.

    Where it fits The usual lunar-ingress search.

    Call jme_mooncross_ut(x2cross, jd_ut, flags, tret, error)
    Arguments
    • x2cross Ecliptic longitude to reach, in degrees.
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • tret Caller-owned array of Julian dates. The description says which index is which event.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_mooncross_node

    What it does Finds when the Moon next reaches its node, on the Terrestrial Time entry.

    When to use it Use this when the start instant is TT and you want the nodal passage.

    Where it fits Eclipse seasons. The UT entry is jme_mooncross_node_ut.

    Call jme_mooncross_node(jd_ut, flags, tret, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • tret Caller-owned array of Julian dates. The description says which index is which event.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_mooncross_node_ut

    What it does Finds when the Moon next reaches its node, starting from Universal Time.

    When to use it Use this from a civil date.

    Where it fits The UT pair of jme_mooncross_node.

    Call jme_mooncross_node_ut(jd_ut, flags, tret, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • tret Caller-owned array of Julian dates. The description says which index is which event.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_helio_cross

    What it does Finds when a body's heliocentric longitude next reaches a target, on the Terrestrial Time entry.

    When to use it Use this for a heliocentric ingress when you have TT.

    Where it fits Outer-planet heliocentric work. The UT entry is jme_helio_cross_ut.

    Call jme_helio_cross(body, x2cross, jd_ut, flags, tret, error)
    Arguments
    • body Body id such as JME_BODY_SUN. The body constants list every id.
    • x2cross Ecliptic longitude to reach, in degrees.
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • tret Caller-owned array of Julian dates. The description says which index is which event.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_helio_cross_ut

    What it does Finds when a body's heliocentric longitude next reaches a target, starting from Universal Time.

    When to use it Use this when the clock is UT.

    Where it fits The UT pair of jme_helio_cross.

    Call jme_helio_cross_ut(body, x2cross, jd_ut, flags, tret, error)
    Arguments
    • body Body id such as JME_BODY_SUN. The body constants list every id.
    • x2cross Ecliptic longitude to reach, in degrees.
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • tret Caller-owned array of Julian dates. The description says which index is which event.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_heliacal_ut

    What it does Searches heliacal rising or setting phenomena at a place.

    When to use it Use this for first or last visibility, not for the geometric sunrise.

    Where it fits A visibility calendar. dat_hel carries the shared atmosphere and object inputs.

    Call jme_heliacal_ut(jd_ut, geopos, dat_hel, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • geopos Observer longitude, latitude, and height, in that order, in degrees and metres.
    • dat_hel Caller-owned array of the shared heliacal inputs: place, atmosphere, and object data.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_vis_limit_mag

    What it does Estimates the limiting visual magnitude at a place and time.

    When to use it Use this to decide whether an object is bright enough to see in those conditions.

    Where it fits Before or beside a heliacal call, with the same dat_hel inputs.

    Call jme_vis_limit_mag(jd_ut, geopos, dat_hel, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • geopos Observer longitude, latitude, and height, in that order, in degrees and metres.
    • dat_hel Caller-owned array of the shared heliacal inputs: place, atmosphere, and object data.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_heliacal_angle

    What it does Returns the heliacal angle used by the visibility routines.

    When to use it Use this when you need that angle itself rather than a search time.

    Where it fits A visibility diagram.

    Call jme_heliacal_angle(jd_ut, geopos, dat_hel, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • geopos Observer longitude, latitude, and height, in that order, in degrees and metres.
    • dat_hel Caller-owned array of the shared heliacal inputs: place, atmosphere, and object data.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_topo_arcus_visionis

    What it does Returns the topocentric arcus visionis for the heliacal inputs.

    When to use it Use this when a traditional visibility rule asks for the arcus visionis.

    Where it fits The same dat_hel setup as the other heliacal calls.

    Call jme_topo_arcus_visionis(jd_ut, geopos, dat_hel, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • geopos Observer longitude, latitude, and height, in that order, in degrees and metres.
    • dat_hel Caller-owned array of the shared heliacal inputs: place, atmosphere, and object data.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    Function group

    Sidereal, Ayanamsa, and Time

    Use these for the clock and the zodiac: Julian dates, Delta-T, sidereal time, and the ayanamsa. Most position calls take a Julian date you build here.

    jme_set_sidereal_mode

    What it does Selects the ayanamsa used by later sidereal longitudes.

    When to use it Call it before a calculation that passes JME_CALC_SIDEREAL, or before an ayanamsa read that should follow the library setting.

    Where it fits Once per chart style. For a user ayanamsa, pass JME_SIDEREAL_USER with t0 and ayan_t0.

    Call jme_set_sidereal_mode(sidereal_mode, t0, ayan_t0)
    Arguments
    • sidereal_mode Ayanamsa id from the JME_SIDEREAL_* constants.
    • t0 Reference epoch for a user ayanamsa, as a Julian date.
    • ayan_t0 Ayanamsa at t0, in degrees, for the user mode.
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_get_sidereal_mode

    What it does Reads the ayanamsa id and the user-mode epoch back out.

    When to use it Call it when another part of the program must follow the mode already set.

    Where it fits After jme_set_sidereal_mode.

    Call jme_get_sidereal_mode(sidereal_mode, t0, ayan_t0)
    Arguments
    • sidereal_mode Ayanamsa id from the JME_SIDEREAL_* constants.
    • t0 Reference epoch for a user ayanamsa, as a Julian date.
    • ayan_t0 Ayanamsa at t0, in degrees, for the user mode.
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_set_delta_t_userdef

    What it does Fixes Delta-T at a constant number of seconds.

    When to use it Use this when you must force TT minus UT, for a test or a historical convention.

    Where it fits A non-finite dt clears the override and returns to the model.

    Call jme_set_delta_t_userdef(dt)
    Arguments
    • dt Delta-T in seconds. A non-finite value clears a user-defined Delta-T.
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_get_ayanamsa_name

    What it does Returns the display name of an ayanamsa id.

    When to use it Use this to label a JME_SIDEREAL_* value in a menu.

    Where it fits A settings screen. The id does not have to be the active mode.

    Call jme_get_ayanamsa_name(model)
    Arguments
    • model Model id from the JME_MODEL_* or JME_SIDEREAL_* constants, depending on the call.
    Result

    Returns a pointer to a static string.

    jme_lmt_to_lat

    What it does Converts local mean time to local apparent time at a longitude.

    When to use it Use this when a clock is mean time and you need apparent solar time.

    Where it fits It applies the equation of time. The reverse is jme_lat_to_lmt.

    Call jme_lmt_to_lat(jd_lmt, geo_lon, jd_lat, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_lmt Local mean time as a Julian date.
    • geo_lon Geographic longitude in degrees. East is positive.
    • jd_lat Local apparent time as a Julian date.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_lat_to_lmt

    What it does Converts local apparent time to local mean time at a longitude.

    When to use it Use this when you have sundial time and need mean time.

    Where it fits The reverse of jme_lmt_to_lat.

    Call jme_lat_to_lmt(jd_lat, geo_lon, jd_lmt, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_lat Local apparent time as a Julian date.
    • geo_lon Geographic longitude in degrees. East is positive.
    • jd_lmt Local mean time as a Julian date.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_centiseconds_to_time_string

    What it does Formats a count of centiseconds as a clock string.

    When to use it Use this to print a duration or a time of day you already hold in centiseconds.

    Where it fits Display only. It does not compute an ephemeris time.

    Call jme_centiseconds_to_time_string(cs, buffer)
    Arguments
    • cs Angle or time in centiseconds. A full circle or a day of time is 1,296,000 centiseconds.
    • buffer Caller-owned character buffer. The call writes the text here.
    Result

    Returns the text. When you pass buffer, the text is written there and the return points at that buffer.

    jme_julian_day

    What it does Builds a Julian date from a calendar date and a decimal hour.

    When to use it Use this to turn a year, month, day, and hour into the jd_ut or jd_et argument of every other call.

    Where it fits The first step of almost every calculation. calendar selects Gregorian or Julian.

    Call jme_julian_day(year, month, day, hour, calendar)
    Arguments
    • year Calendar year. Astronomical year numbering, so 1 BCE is year 0.
    • month Month number from 1 to 12.
    • day Day of the month.
    • hour Hour. Where the call takes a decimal hour, fractions of an hour are allowed.
    • calendar JME_CALENDAR_GREGORIAN or JME_CALENDAR_JULIAN.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_calendar_is_leap_year

    What it does Reports whether a year is a leap year in the selected calendar.

    When to use it Use this before you accept 29 February.

    Where it fits Date entry. It does not convert a Julian date.

    Call jme_calendar_is_leap_year(year, calendar)
    Arguments
    • year Calendar year. Astronomical year numbering, so 1 BCE is year 0.
    • calendar JME_CALENDAR_GREGORIAN or JME_CALENDAR_JULIAN.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_date_is_valid

    What it does Reports whether year, month, and day exist in the selected calendar.

    When to use it Use this to reject a date before you call jme_julian_day.

    Where it fits Form validation.

    Call jme_date_is_valid(year, month, day, calendar)
    Arguments
    • year Calendar year. Astronomical year numbering, so 1 BCE is year 0.
    • month Month number from 1 to 12.
    • day Day of the month.
    • calendar JME_CALENDAR_GREGORIAN or JME_CALENDAR_JULIAN.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_day_of_year

    What it does Returns the day number within the year, starting at 1.

    When to use it Use this for a day-of-year display or a seasonal index.

    Where it fits After the date is known to be valid.

    Call jme_day_of_year(year, month, day, calendar)
    Arguments
    • year Calendar year. Astronomical year numbering, so 1 BCE is year 0.
    • month Month number from 1 to 12.
    • day Day of the month.
    • calendar JME_CALENDAR_GREGORIAN or JME_CALENDAR_JULIAN.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_day_of_week

    What it does Returns the weekday of a Julian date.

    When to use it Use this for a calendar label. The numbering is the library's weekday index.

    Where it fits Any date you already converted.

    Call jme_day_of_week(jd)
    Arguments
    • jd Julian date. The description of the call says which time scale that number is.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    jme_reverse_julian_day

    What it does Splits a Julian date back into calendar year, month, day, and decimal hour.

    When to use it Use this to display a Julian date you computed, such as a rise time.

    Where it fits The inverse of jme_julian_day. For UTC fields including minutes and seconds, use jme_jd_to_utc.

    Call jme_reverse_julian_day(jd, calendar, year, month, day, hour)
    Arguments
    • jd Julian date. The description of the call says which time scale that number is.
    • calendar JME_CALENDAR_GREGORIAN or JME_CALENDAR_JULIAN.
    • year Calendar year. Astronomical year numbering, so 1 BCE is year 0.
    • month Month number from 1 to 12.
    • day Day of the month.
    • hour Hour. Where the call takes a decimal hour, fractions of an hour are allowed.
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_delta_t

    What it does Returns Delta-T, TT minus UT, in seconds for a Universal Time date, using the active model.

    When to use it Use this when you have UT and need TT, or you need to show Delta-T.

    Where it fits The model-selecting form is jme_delta_t_ex.

    Call jme_delta_t(jd_ut)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_delta_t_ex

    What it does Returns Delta-T for an explicit model.

    When to use it Use this when the caller chooses the series, including JME_TIME_DELTAT_AUTOMATIC.

    Where it fits Models whose source tables are not in the library return a non-finite value and an error.

    Call jme_delta_t_ex(jd_ut, model, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • model Model id from the JME_MODEL_* or JME_SIDEREAL_* constants, depending on the call.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_get_ayanamsa

    What it does Returns the active ayanamsa at Terrestrial Time.

    When to use it Use this to subtract from a tropical longitude when you want the sidereal longitude of the current mode.

    Where it fits The mode comes from jme_set_sidereal_mode. The UT form is jme_get_ayanamsa_ut.

    Call jme_get_ayanamsa(jd_et)
    Arguments
    • jd_et Terrestrial Time (TT) as a Julian date.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_get_ayanamsa_ut

    What it does Returns the active ayanamsa at Universal Time.

    When to use it Use this when the clock is UT.

    Where it fits The UT pair of jme_get_ayanamsa.

    Call jme_get_ayanamsa_ut(jd_ut)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_get_ayanamsa_ex

    What it does Returns one named ayanamsa at Terrestrial Time, without changing the active mode.

    When to use it Use this to compare two ayanamsas, or to label a model you have not selected.

    Where it fits model is a JME_SIDEREAL_* id.

    Call jme_get_ayanamsa_ex(jd_et, model, ayan, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_et Terrestrial Time (TT) as a Julian date.
    • model Model id from the JME_MODEL_* or JME_SIDEREAL_* constants, depending on the call.
    • ayan Receives the ayanamsa in degrees.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_get_ayanamsa_ex_ut

    What it does Returns one named ayanamsa at Universal Time.

    When to use it Use this when the clock is UT and the mode is an argument, not the library setting.

    Where it fits The UT pair of jme_get_ayanamsa_ex.

    Call jme_get_ayanamsa_ex_ut(jd_ut, model, ayan, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • model Model id from the JME_MODEL_* or JME_SIDEREAL_* constants, depending on the call.
    • ayan Receives the ayanamsa in degrees.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_time_equ

    What it does Returns the equation of time at Universal Time.

    When to use it Use this to move between mean solar time and apparent solar time.

    Where it fits jme_lmt_to_lat uses the same quantity. e receives the value.

    Call jme_time_equ(jd_ut, e, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • e Receives the equation of time.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_jd_to_utc

    What it does Splits a Julian date into UTC calendar fields, including minutes and seconds.

    When to use it Use this to display a computed instant on a civil clock.

    Where it fits calendar selects Gregorian or Julian. For a decimal hour only, jme_reverse_julian_day is enough.

    Call jme_jd_to_utc(jd, calendar, year, month, day, hour, minute, second)
    Arguments
    • jd Julian date. The description of the call says which time scale that number is.
    • calendar JME_CALENDAR_GREGORIAN or JME_CALENDAR_JULIAN.
    • year Calendar year. Astronomical year numbering, so 1 BCE is year 0.
    • month Month number from 1 to 12.
    • day Day of the month.
    • hour Hour. Where the call takes a decimal hour, fractions of an hour are allowed.
    • minute Minute.
    • second Second, including the fraction. A leap second 60 is accepted only on a UTC path that validates it.
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_sidereal_time

    What it does Returns Greenwich sidereal time in hours for a Universal Time date.

    When to use it Use this when you need RAMC's starting point and you do not need a status code.

    Where it fits The explicit mean-or-apparent form is jme_sidereal_time_ex.

    Call jme_sidereal_time(jd_ut)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_sidereal_time0

    What it does Returns Greenwich sidereal time from UT, an obliquity, and a nutation you already have.

    When to use it Use this when you computed eps and nut yourself and you do not want the call to look them up.

    Where it fits A custom precession pipeline.

    Call jme_sidereal_time0(jd_ut, eps, nut)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • eps Obliquity of the ecliptic, in degrees, at the date you are using.
    • nut Nutation contribution already computed, in the unit this sidereal-time call expects.
    Result

    Returns the number described above. A non-finite value means the call could not produce that number.

    jme_utc_time_zone

    What it does Shifts a UTC calendar time by a timezone offset in hours.

    When to use it Use this to present an instant in local civil time, or to convert a local civil time toward UTC.

    Where it fits timezone is hours east of UTC. This is a clock shift, not the equation of time.

    Call jme_utc_time_zone(year, month, day, hour, minute, second, timezone, out_year, out_month, out_day, out_hour, out_minute, out_second)
    Arguments
    • year Calendar year. Astronomical year numbering, so 1 BCE is year 0.
    • month Month number from 1 to 12.
    • day Day of the month.
    • hour Hour. Where the call takes a decimal hour, fractions of an hour are allowed.
    • minute Minute.
    • second Second, including the fraction. A leap second 60 is accepted only on a UTC path that validates it.
    • timezone Hours east of UTC. West longitudes use a negative offset.
    • out_year Receives the converted year.
    • out_month Receives the converted month.
    • out_day Receives the converted day.
    • out_hour Receives the converted hour.
    • out_minute Receives the converted minute.
    • out_second Receives the converted second.
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_utc_to_jd

    What it does Converts a UTC calendar time to a UTC Julian date.

    When to use it Use this when the input is UTC wall time, including a possible leap second, and you need a Julian date.

    Where it fits Dates after the leap-second table fail. jme_julian_day does not apply the leap-second table.

    Call jme_utc_to_jd(year, month, day, hour, minute, second, calendar, jd_utc)
    Arguments
    • year Calendar year. Astronomical year numbering, so 1 BCE is year 0.
    • month Month number from 1 to 12.
    • day Day of the month.
    • hour Hour. Where the call takes a decimal hour, fractions of an hour are allowed.
    • minute Minute.
    • second Second, including the fraction. A leap second 60 is accepted only on a UTC path that validates it.
    • calendar JME_CALENDAR_GREGORIAN or JME_CALENDAR_JULIAN.
    • jd_utc Receives the UTC Julian date.
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    Function group

    Added in 1.1.0

    These entered in 1.1.0 and stay in 2.0.0. Use them when you need an explicit time scale, a mean or true ayanamsa, Gauquelin sectors, polar motion, or a checked setter.

    Time scales

    jme_time_scale_convert

    What it does Converts a split Julian date from one time scale to another.

    When to use it Use this when you must move among UT, TAI, TT, TDB, TCG, and TCB yourself.

    Where it fits High-level jme_calc_ut already converts UT. UTC on this call follows the leap-second table, which currently stops at 2027-06-30.

    Call jme_time_scale_convert(jd1, jd2, from_scale, to_scale, out1, out2, error)
    Arguments
    • jd1 First part of a split Julian date.
    • jd2 Second part of a split Julian date. The instant is jd1 + jd2.
    • from_scale Source time scale, one of the JME_TIME_SCALE_* constants.
    • to_scale Time scale to convert into, one of the JME_TIME_SCALE_* constants.
    • out1 Receives the first part of the converted split Julian date.
    • out2 Receives the second part of the converted split Julian date.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_time_scale_name

    What it does Returns the display name of a time-scale id.

    When to use it Use this to label a JME_TIME_SCALE_* value.

    Where it fits A time-scale menu.

    Call jme_time_scale_name(scale)
    Arguments
    • scale Time-scale id from the JME_TIME_SCALE_* constants.
    Result

    Returns the text. When you pass buffer, the text is written there and the return points at that buffer.

    jme_leap_second_table_info

    What it does Reports how far the embedded UTC leap-second table extends.

    When to use it Call it before you convert a future UTC date, so you can fail clearly past the table.

    Where it fits The covered range currently ends at 2027-06-30 UTC.

    Call jme_leap_second_table_info(jd_utc_valid_until, last_tai_minus_utc, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_utc_valid_until Receives the first UTC Julian date the leap-second table does not cover.
    • last_tai_minus_utc Receives the latest TAI minus UTC, in seconds.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_delta_t_iers_table_info

    What it does Reports the first, last observed, and last predicted dates of the embedded IERS Delta-T table.

    When to use it Call it when you need to know whether a date is observed, predicted, or outside the IERS file.

    Where it fits Automatic Delta-T uses this table where it covers the date.

    Call jme_delta_t_iers_table_info(jd_first, jd_last_observed, jd_last, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_first Receives the first Julian date in the table.
    • jd_last_observed Receives the last Julian date marked as observed.
    • jd_last Receives the last Julian date in the table, including predictions.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_sidereal_time_ex

    What it does Returns Greenwich sidereal time in hours, mean or apparent, with a status.

    When to use it Use this when a failure, such as a bad Delta-T, must be an error rather than a bare number.

    Where it fits apparent is zero for mean time and non-zero for apparent time. hours receives the result.

    Call jme_sidereal_time_ex(jd_ut, apparent, hours, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • apparent Zero asks for mean sidereal time. Non-zero asks for apparent sidereal time.
    • hours Receives sidereal time in hours.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    Sidereal

    jme_get_ayanamsa_ex2

    What it does Returns a named ayanamsa at Terrestrial Time, and optionally its rate, with mean or true equinox chosen by flags.

    When to use it Use this when the chart must say whether the ayanamsa is mean or true.

    Where it fits flags is JME_AYANAMSA_MEAN or JME_AYANAMSA_TRUE. rate may be omitted.

    Call jme_get_ayanamsa_ex2(jd_et, model, flags, ayan, rate, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_et Terrestrial Time (TT) as a Julian date.
    • model Model id from the JME_MODEL_* or JME_SIDEREAL_* constants, depending on the call.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • ayan Receives the ayanamsa in degrees.
    • rate Receives the rate of change. You may pass an empty pointer when you do not need it.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_get_ayanamsa_ex2_ut

    What it does Returns a named mean or true ayanamsa at Universal Time, and optionally its rate.

    When to use it Use this when the clock is UT.

    Where it fits The UT pair of jme_get_ayanamsa_ex2.

    Call jme_get_ayanamsa_ex2_ut(jd_ut, model, flags, ayan, rate, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • model Model id from the JME_MODEL_* or JME_SIDEREAL_* constants, depending on the call.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • ayan Receives the ayanamsa in degrees.
    • rate Receives the rate of change. You may pass an empty pointer when you do not need it.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    Houses

    jme_houses_gauquelin

    What it does Computes the 36 Gauquelin sector cusps at Universal Time.

    When to use it Use this for Gauquelin sectors. Do not pass JME_HOUSE_GAUQUELIN to jme_houses.

    Where it fits A sector wheel. cusps needs 37 numbers. Polar latitudes, where a semi-arc is undefined, return JME_ERR.

    Call jme_houses_gauquelin(jd_ut, flags, geo_lat, geo_lon, cusps, ascmc, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_ut Universal Time as a Julian date. Use this when the clock you have is UT.
    • flags Flag bits for this call. Pass 0 for the default. The constant group for this family lists the bits.
    • geo_lat Geographic latitude in degrees. North is positive.
    • geo_lon Geographic longitude in degrees. East is positive.
    • cusps Caller-owned cusp array. Twelve-cusp calls use 13 numbers (index 1 to 12). Gauquelin calls use 37 numbers.
    • ascmc Caller-owned array for the Ascendant, Midheaven, and the other angles this call returns.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_houses_gauquelin_armc

    What it does Computes the 36 Gauquelin sector cusps from RAMC and obliquity.

    When to use it Use this when you already have RAMC.

    Where it fits The RAMC pair of jme_houses_gauquelin. Same 37-cusp array.

    Call jme_houses_gauquelin_armc(armc, geo_lat, eps, cusps, ascmc, error)
    Arguments
    • armc Right ascension of the Midheaven, in degrees.
    • geo_lat Geographic latitude in degrees. North is positive.
    • eps Obliquity of the ecliptic, in degrees, at the date you are using.
    • cusps Caller-owned cusp array. Twelve-cusp calls use 13 numbers (index 1 to 12). Gauquelin calls use 37 numbers.
    • ascmc Caller-owned array for the Ascendant, Midheaven, and the other angles this call returns.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    Engine policy

    jme_calc_resolve_engine

    What it does Reports which engine jme_calc will use for a body at a Terrestrial Time.

    When to use it Use this when ENGINE=AUTO must not switch models silently, and you want the choice in advance.

    Where it fits engine_id receives JPL, Moshier, or VSOP87 plus ELP. The substituted flag is 1 when a barycentre replaced a planet centre.

    Call jme_calc_resolve_engine(jd_et, body, engine_id, jpl_center_substituted, error)
    Arguments
    • jd_et Terrestrial Time (TT) as a Julian date.
    • body Body id such as JME_BODY_SUN. The body constants list every id.
    • engine_id Receives the engine id: JPL, Moshier, or VSOP87 plus ELP.
    • jpl_center_substituted Receives 1 when a missing planet centre was replaced by its system barycentre.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_set_jpl_center_policy

    What it does Chooses what happens when a JPL planet centre is not in the open kernels.

    When to use it Use JME_JPL_CENTER_STRICT, the default, when a missing centre must be an error. Use BARYCENTER only when the system barycentre is an acceptable stand-in.

    Where it fits Before jme_calc in JPL or AUTO mode. A bad value leaves the previous policy in place.

    Call jme_set_jpl_center_policy(policy, error)
    Arguments
    • policy JME_JPL_CENTER_STRICT or JME_JPL_CENTER_BARYCENTER.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_get_jpl_center_policy

    What it does Returns the active planet-centre policy.

    When to use it Call it before you interpret a JPL position of Mars through Pluto.

    Where it fits After jme_set_jpl_center_policy.

    Call jme_get_jpl_center_policy()
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    Validating setters

    jme_set_astro_models_checked

    What it does Sets model tokens and rejects an unknown or over-long token.

    When to use it Use this instead of jme_set_astro_models when a bad string must not change anything.

    Where it fits Startup from user input. On JME_ERR the previous models stay.

    Call jme_set_astro_models_checked(models, error)
    Arguments
    • models Text tokens such as ENGINE=JPL or ENGINE=MOSHIER. The engine section lists the tokens.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_set_topo_checked

    What it does Stores the observer and rejects a non-finite value or a latitude outside -90 to 90.

    When to use it Use this when the place comes from a form.

    Where it fits On JME_ERR the previous observer stays. Longitude is wrapped.

    Call jme_set_topo_checked(lon, lat, altitude, error)
    Arguments
    • lon Longitude in degrees. East is positive when this is a place. For an angle helper it is the ecliptic or equatorial longitude the call names.
    • lat Latitude in degrees. North is positive when this is a place.
    • altitude Height. For an observer this is metres. For refraction this is the altitude angle in degrees.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_set_sidereal_mode_checked

    What it does Selects an ayanamsa and rejects an unknown mode or a non-finite epoch.

    When to use it Use this when the mode comes from a form.

    Where it fits On JME_ERR the previous mode stays.

    Call jme_set_sidereal_mode_checked(sidereal_mode, t0, ayan_t0, error)
    Arguments
    • sidereal_mode Ayanamsa id from the JME_SIDEREAL_* constants.
    • t0 Reference epoch for a user ayanamsa, as a Julian date.
    • ayan_t0 Ayanamsa at t0, in degrees, for the user mode.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    Earth orientation (polar motion)

    jme_eop_load_file

    What it does Loads an Earth-orientation file of polar motion.

    When to use it Call it before you ask for topocentric places that should include polar motion.

    Where it fits The file supplies x and y. jme_set_polar_motion turns the correction on.

    Call jme_eop_load_file(path, error)
    Arguments
    • path Filesystem path. For a kernel this is the .bsp file or the directory that holds it.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_eop_clear

    What it does Drops the loaded Earth-orientation table.

    When to use it Call it when a later calculation must not use the file you loaded.

    Where it fits After a chart that needed polar motion, if the next chart must not inherit it.

    Call jme_eop_clear()
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_eop_coverage

    What it does Reports the first and last modified Julian dates in the loaded Earth-orientation table.

    When to use it Call it before you evaluate a date, so you know the date is inside the file.

    Where it fits After jme_eop_load_file.

    Call jme_eop_coverage(mjd_first, mjd_last, error)
    Arguments
    • mjd_first Receives the first modified Julian date in the Earth-orientation file.
    • mjd_last Receives the last modified Julian date in the Earth-orientation file.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_eop_polar_motion

    What it does Interpolates polar motion x and y at a modified Julian date.

    When to use it Use this to read the angles yourself, or to check a date before enabling the correction.

    Where it fits predicted is non-zero when a prediction row was used.

    Call jme_eop_polar_motion(mjd, xp_arcsec, yp_arcsec, predicted, error)
    Arguments
    • mjd Modified Julian date of the Earth-orientation row you want.
    • xp_arcsec Receives polar motion x, in arcseconds.
    • yp_arcsec Receives polar motion y, in arcseconds.
    • predicted Receives non-zero when a predicted row was used.
    • error Caller-owned text buffer. On failure the library writes the reason here.
    Result

    Returns JME_OK (0) or JME_ERR (-1). On JME_ERR, read error. The output arguments are written as the description says.

    jme_set_polar_motion

    What it does Turns polar motion on or off for later topocentric work.

    When to use it Turn it on only after a file is loaded and the date is inside that file.

    Where it fits It affects observer position, horizontal coordinates, and eclipse geography.

    Call jme_set_polar_motion(enabled)
    Arguments
    • enabled Non-zero applies polar motion. Zero leaves the observer on the ellipsoid without it.
    Result

    Returns nothing. The call writes its output arguments, or it changes a library setting for later calls.

    jme_get_polar_motion

    What it does Returns whether polar motion is currently applied.

    When to use it Call it before you interpret a topocentric altitude.

    Where it fits After jme_set_polar_motion.

    Call jme_get_polar_motion()
    Result

    Returns the integer result named above. A status-style return uses JME_OK and JME_ERR.

    Function group

    Behaviour changes in 1.1.0

    Read this before you compare a result with a build from before 1.1.0. The items are changes in existing models, not new function names.

    • Precession model PREC=LASKAR1986 (JME_MODEL_PREC_LASKAR_1986) now returns a matrix (Laskar 1986 Tables 5 and 8) instead of an error.
    • JME_MODEL_DELTAT_STEPHENSON_ETC_2016 is now the published 2016 Table S15; JME_TIME_DELTAT_AUTOMATIC uses the 2021 revision before the IERS table.
    • With the DE441 tidal selector (jme_set_tid_acc(JME_TIME_TIDAL_DE441)), historical (pre-1955) Delta-T returns NaN and an error naming Park et al. 2021, because no DE441 lunar tidal acceleration has been published. JME_TIME_TIDAL_AUTOMATIC applies no correction.
    • The tidal correction is never applied to IERS observed/predicted values or to a user-fixed Delta-T.
    • Delta-T models SM1984 and S1997 stay refused with explicit errors (sources unavailable).

    Reference

    478 Public Constants

    Public JME_* constants from the C headers. The same names are exported by PHP, Python, and Dart. JME_JME_H and JME_EXTENDED_H are header include guards, not calculation constants. The bindings still export those two guards. The Use column says what the constant means and which call receives it.

    This box filters the constant list. The sidebar search looks through the whole page and highlights each match.

    Constant group

    Additional Constants

    Coordinate ids and other values that did not fall in a narrower group. Pass a coordinate id only to the call that documents it, such as refraction.

    Constant Value Use
    JME_COORD_APPARENT_TO_TRUE 289 Refraction direction. Pass this as calc_flag to jme_refract or jme_refract_extended to remove refraction and turn an apparent altitude into a true altitude.
    JME_COORD_ECLIPTIC_TO_HORIZONTAL 290 Name of the ecliptic-to-horizon conversion. The functions that perform the pieces are jme_ecliptic_to_equatorial and jme_equatorial_to_horizontal.
    JME_COORD_EQUATORIAL_TO_HORIZONTAL 291 Name of the equator-to-horizon conversion. The call is jme_equatorial_to_horizontal.
    JME_COORD_HORIZONTAL_TO_ECLIPTIC 292 Name of the horizon-to-ecliptic conversion. Go through jme_horizontal_to_equatorial and then jme_equatorial_to_ecliptic.
    JME_COORD_HORIZONTAL_TO_EQUATORIAL 293 Name of the horizon-to-equator conversion. The call is jme_horizontal_to_equatorial.
    JME_COORD_TRUE_TO_APPARENT 294 Refraction direction. Pass this as calc_flag to add refraction and turn a true altitude into an apparent altitude.

    Constant group

    Angle and Formatting Constants

    Pass a rounding id to jme_split_degree when you print a degree angle. ROUND_DEG, ROUND_MIN, and ROUND_SEC are the values that call applies.

    Constant Value Use
    JME_ANGLE_FORMAT_KEEP_DEG 0 Angle-format id for keeping the degree field. jme_split_degree itself applies only the ROUND_DEG, ROUND_MIN, and ROUND_SEC ids.
    JME_ANGLE_FORMAT_KEEP_SIGN 1 Angle-format id for keeping the sign. jme_split_degree returns the sign separately in isgn.
    JME_ANGLE_FORMAT_NAKSHATRA 2 Angle-format id naming a nakshatra-style display. It is not a nakshatra calculation. Longitude boundaries still come from jme_mooncross_ut.
    JME_ANGLE_FORMAT_ROUND_DEG 3 Round a split angle to the nearest degree. Pass this as roundflag to jme_split_degree.
    JME_ANGLE_FORMAT_ROUND_MIN 4 Round a split angle to the nearest arcminute. Pass this as roundflag to jme_split_degree.
    JME_ANGLE_FORMAT_ROUND_SEC 5 Round a split angle to the nearest arcsecond. Pass this as roundflag to jme_split_degree.
    JME_ANGLE_FORMAT_ZODIACAL 6 Angle-format id for a sign-and-degree display. It does not compute a sign. Normalise the longitude first, then split it.

    Constant group
